accepted_deviations.summary: Profile-relay assignment hashes the pubkey, so two contacts can land on the same pool relay; collisions follow the birthday bound (~79% for a 5-member roster over the 8-relay pool). Collision-free-per-roster assignment would require the profile module to know roster membership, which its import boundary forbids by design.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim 'no relay ever learns two members of the same circle', nor 'no single server sees everyone you look up'. The spreading claim must stay statistical and must keep the collision sentence beside it.

accepted_deviations.summary: A peer's assignment salt is private to their install, so Haven cannot know which pool relay a peer reads from; publishing the user's own kind-0 therefore targets the ENTIRE usable pool. Every pool relay learns (our pubkey, our IP), and one that also serves our reads can link identity to our ~1/N contact sample.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim profile publishing is limited to a subset of the pool, nor that profile publishing is unlinkable to the identity. It MAY state that reads are unauthenticated (the fetch path is built with no signer and structurally cannot answer NIP-42).

accepted_deviations.summary: Haven publishes no NIP-65 / kind-10002 relay list naming the profile pool, because that event is identity-signed and publicly fetchable and would rebuild the cross-plane link the pool exists to break. Accepted cost: outbox-model external clients may fail to resolve a Haven profile. Enforced by check_profile_privacy_boundaries.sh Check 10 and by RelayType::Profile::to_kind() returning None.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not imply that no relay can ever learn a device uses it for the profile plane — a pool relay sees that traffic directly. Only the narrower claim is true: Haven never publishes a list naming the profile relays, so a relay OUTSIDE the pool has no public pointer to it.

accepted_deviations.summary: The kind-0 merge base is fetched from the profile pool only — a deliberate reversal of the MEDIUM-4 fix (self_merge_base_relays deleted). A Haven save can therefore drop kind-0 fields another client set on relays outside the pool.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that editing your profile in Haven preserves everything set by another Nostr client. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this today — see the report's disclosure-gap section; no invariant references P4 because filing one would require inventing a disclosure that does not exist.

accepted_deviations.summary: The per-install profile-relay assignment salt is NEVER rotated: rotation discloses each contact to an additional relay, converging on full disclosure, so a stable salt is strictly better in aggregate. Accepted cost: the assigned relay accumulates a durable 'this IP is persistently interested in this pubkey' observation. Bounded by PROFILE_MAX_RELAY_RANK = 2 and destroyed by two distinct paths (wipe_all_profiles; deletion of the circles.db file set).
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present the stable pairing as a pure benefit, and must not claim the pairing 'never changes' — the retry ladder reaches a second relay and rendezvous ranking shifts when the pool changes. State the bound as at most TWO of the eight, and keep the durable-record cost sentence alongside the spreading claim.

accepted_deviations.summary: Haven ships no Tor or proxy support. A pool relay, a circle relay, the tile provider and any host serving a co-member's profile picture all observe the user's real IP on publish and on read. The salted partition limits WHAT a relay learns, not WHO it is talking to.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must make no network-level unlinkability or anonymity claim, and must never say Haven hides your IP address. A VPN may be described as the mitigation, attributed to the VPN, never to Haven.

accepted_deviations.summary: Owner-approved with the relay-plane segregation on 2026-10-31 (plan D11). Every circle Haven creates without named relays sits on three relays drawn from PRODUCTION_LOCATION_RELAYS, a list only Haven uses, and every member of that circle dials the same three. A network observer who sees DNS queries or TLS SNI can therefore infer from those hostnames that a device runs Haven and that devices dialling the same three are probably in one circle, where a default circle used to ride the account seed (relay.damus.io, relay.primal.net, nos.lol) that most Nostr clients dial; and the pool's operators together can enumerate Haven users' IP addresses, because the pool is Haven-specific. The same-IP-across-planes residual is unchanged (P6). Mitigation: none beyond the recorded absence of network-level unlinkability.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that the relays a circle uses reveal nothing about which app you use or about who shares a circle with you, and must not present Haven's choice of circle relays as hiding Haven use from the network. A VPN may be described as hiding the destination from the local network, attributed to the VPN, never to Haven.

accepted_deviations.summary: The contamination ledger is append-only because contamination is historical — a relay that routed a circle's kind-445 last month saw those events, and leaving does not un-see them. Welcome-delivery relays were persisted nowhere before the change, so refresh_contamination_ledger cannot fold them in and will not exclude them.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that leaving a circle removes all relay exposure, nor that the contamination warnings cover every relay that has ever carried this identity's traffic.

accepted_deviations.summary: Periodic leaf-key self-update (a MIP-03 SHOULD) is disabled (PeriodicMaintenancePolicy::Disabled at every open). The post-join self-update protocol-core/joining.md asks for 'as soon as practical' IS made: once, from the obligation MDK records at every join, in a foreground full drive after catch-up and MDK's grace, quiet and jitter windows. After that a member's leaf rotates only on its own repair or a commit of its own carrying an update path, never on a timer.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must never say keys rotate regularly or periodically, and must never use this locale's term for forward secrecy. Key change may only be described as following a membership change, one's own join, or an explicit repair. The spec's own words support this: 'a member who never rotates is a forward-secrecy weakness for itself' (protocol-core/joining.md).

accepted_deviations.summary: NOT one connection per relay: Haven opens at least TWO long-lived nostr-sdk Clients per process — the live-sync engine's receive client (build_engine_client, haven-core/src/relay/live_sync/session.rs:111) and the publish client (RelayManager::new, haven-core/src/relay/manager.rs:613) — plus the live session's own fanout drive pool while one runs (LiveSyncCore::new_local) and one more for every isolate that builds its own RelayManager, which the Android background-sharing foreground service does. A shared relay therefore sees up to three connections from the foreground isolate alone, not one, and can join them by source address without any protocol help. A relay serving BOTH the gift-wrap inbox (kind 1059 by #p = user pubkey) and group messages (kind 445 by #h = nostr_group_id) over the same connection can correlate the real identity pubkey with circle membership by connection continuity. Since M11 the receive connection is STANDING while the app is FOREGROUNDED, on both platforms, so the correlation is continuous rather than bursty for as long as that socket is held. Since P4 it is no longer standing while backgrounded on iOS either: with background sharing on the engine is PAUSED between publishes and both filters ride one bounded burst per publish tick, so for a CIRCLE relay the join is per-burst rather than continuous. Per-burst is NOT per-publish, though since PUB-COALESCE it is close to it: a burst re-anchors every circle's #h REQ, connects the whole relay union AND publishes every publish-eligible circle, so a circle relay sees a REQ/CLOSE pair on every burst and this device's kind-445 for its own circle on essentially every burst too. The join stays wider than the send in three cases only — a burst whose publish window refuses publishes nothing at all; a subscribed circle that is not publish-eligible (quarantined because its encrypted state failed to load, or engine-flagged Unrecoverable) is re-anchored on every burst and never published to; a send that fails, is deferred by the engine, or is the tail of a roster past kMaxCirclesPerBurst. What coalescing ADDS to this deviation is a duration: the union connection is held across the whole staggered publish pass, so its connect-to-disconnect span grows with the number of eligible circles and hands EVERY relay in the union — one carrying a single circle, or an inbox relay carrying none — an estimator of that count, which the per-circle schedules leaked only as a rate and only to relays that already read the circle set off the multiplexed #h filter (PUB-COALESCE). That NARROWS the deviation for circle relays without strictly narrowing it: an inbox-ONLY relay (kind-10050 inbox, none of this account's circles — an independent set) carries no kind-445 to correlate with, and where it used to see one continuous socket it now sees a REQ/CLOSE pair every 72-168 s (the 120 s nominal cadence, jittered ±40 %), which is itself the inference "this pubkey is background-sharing right now". The lever is INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ (OD4-b, accepted, blocked on a separate defect and not yet raised); at the shipped value that inference is a named, disclosed residual, not a mitigated one. The residuals P4 carries are enumerated in SECURITY.md under "iOS background sharing: presence only at publish instants (P4)". On Android it no longer outlives the foreground: since P1 the pause path stops the engine in BOTH toggle states (with sharing ON it stops first to hand the MLS session to the foreground service; with sharing OFF `_stopLiveSyncBounded()` stops it and deliberately does not release the guard, since no isolate reclaims it), and the resume heal restarts it. Not protocol-forced: the kind-10050 inbox list and the group's 0x8004 relay set are independent. Seeding them disjointly was declined at first, for the connection count and because P6 (no Tor/proxy) leaves IP-level joining intact, and re-decided on 2026-10-31 (the relay-plane segregation, whose owner decision OD-3 accepted the extra sockets, ESTIMATED in POWER_EFFICIENCY_PLAN.md §6.5a): a circle Haven creates without named relays now takes its relays from the location pool, never one on its creator's own lists, so for such a circle the single-socket join is gone unless a member's own lists name one of its relays. It remains for every circle created before that change and for circles other clients create; P6 still leaves IP-level joining intact.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim relays cannot link your identity to your circle membership, and must not present the ephemeral per-message kind-445 author keys as making you unlinkable at the relay.

accepted_deviations.summary: Per-circle publish schedules are replaced by ONE coalesced burst per jittered interval that publishes every publish-eligible circle, so radio wakes fall from about N x 30/h to about 30/h. Shared-relay decorrelation was never effective while the multiplexed #h subscription and the single publish socket exist — a shared relay reads the circle set straight off the filter — so what is given up is only weak protection against colluding relays that ignore IP. THREE costs are accepted. (1) RECORDED: with one shared tick sequence, circles held on DISJOINT relay sets emit identical inter-burst intervals, so anyone holding two of your circles' relay archives — each relay carrying only ONE of those circles — can tell the two circles belong to the same phone. (2) The circle COUNT becomes a single-relay observable, and WHICH SOCKET carries it splits by plane. The burst holds its connection across the whole staggered publish pass, so the span grows with the number of eligible circles. Backgrounded on iOS that connection is the engine socket over the entire relay union (every circle's relays and the inbox relays), measurable server-side by any relay in that union — one carrying only one of your circles, and an inbox-only relay carrying none. On the ANDROID FOREGROUND SERVICE there is no engine socket at all, so the publish pool IS the carrier: RelayManager::shutdown is a COLLECTIVE client.disconnect(), and the service calls it at step 9b of every delivery cycle and again in onDestroy, so a relay carrying exactly one circle in a pass sees connect-at-its-own-publish through disconnect-at-teardown — a tail that grows with the circles published AFTER it and, over the CSPRNG burst permutation, converges to the whole pass length. In the FOREGROUND there is no collective disconnect: publish_relay_options() is ping(false).reconnect(false).sleep_when_idle(true).idle_timeout(10 s), polled once a minute from inside the connection task, so each relay's socket sleeps independently in (60 s, 70 s] after that relay's own last send and measures only its own span. The old scheme leaked N only as a RATE, and only to shared relays that already read it off the multiplexed filter; the new one leaks it as a DURATION, to relays that previously could not know it at all. kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) bounds the roster and therefore the estimator, one circle under the kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11) at which the per-gap ceiling saturates. (3) N ALSO LEAKS THROUGH THE SIGNED TIMESTAMPS, and that carrier persists. PublishStagger.maxGapFor is deterministic and INJECTIVE over n = 5..10, the whole range kMaxCirclesPerAccount admits (only 2, 3 and 4 collapse, all three at the 9 s ceiling), and the expected whole-burst span rises monotonically with it: about 5.5 s at two circles, 11 at three, 16.5 at four, up to 24 s at ten. An observer holding kind-445 archives of two of your circles — exactly the adversary cost (1) hands the LINK to — reads one whole-second delta per burst; over a handful of bursts the largest delta estimates the burst span (monotone in n) and the lowest cluster's upper edge estimates the per-gap ceiling. That ceiling does NOT invert to a single n: created_at is whole seconds and the millisecond injectivity does not survive the quantization, so the observable alphabet resolves the roster exactly at five and six circles, to a PAIR at seven/eight and nine/ten (which share {2..5} and {2,3,4}), and to the TRIPLE two/three/four below that (which share {2..9}). Separating a pair needs the span term or the delta FREQUENCIES rather than the ceiling, i.e. more bursts - a cost in samples and not a bound, so the count still leaks, one bit coarser on those two pairs. A relay carrying several of your circles reads adjacent pairs directly and converges faster. It is worse than cost (2)'s duration in three ways: it needs no socket observation at all (a passive archive scraper suffices), connection noise does not defeat it, and it PERSISTS, because the delta is inside the SIGNED event and therefore in every archive of it. It compounds with cost (1) — link, then count. kMaxCirclesPerAccount bounds the estimate at ten, which is a ceiling on the estimate and not a mitigation. The CSPRNG stagger is retained with its constants unmoved, and its claim is NARROWED TWICE. It is not 'the archive-adversary defence', because after coalescing the archive reader gets the link anyway from the shared inter-burst interval sequence. And what it buys is ROSTER-SCOPED rather than a flat eight values: maxGapFor prices every gap at the burst's OWN size, so the observable whole-second delta alphabet thins monotonically — {2..9} (eight values) up to four circles, {2..6} at six, {2..5} at eight, and {2,3,4} at kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10), the largest burst a bounded roster can produce; maxGapFor keeps answering one circle further, where the alphabet is {2,3}, and no observer reaches that while the bound holds. Coalescing caused the thinning: pre-P5 every gap was priced at the default totalPublishes = 2, so the alphabet was always eight — and the eight-value proof cited on INV-R-PER-CIRCLE-PUBLISH-DECORRELATED draws at that same default, so it pins only the n = 2 case. At small rosters the downgrade in KIND is real: a byte-identical created_at is a zero-cost equality join over a whole-network index (created_at_A == created_at_B, decisive on one burst), while eight admissible offsets force a windowed correlation that needs a targeted hypothesis about which two circles share a device. AT THE ROSTER BOUND IT BARELY IS: a three-element alphabet is three shifted equality joins over that same whole-network index, still un-targeted mass linkage, so what survives at ten circles is a constant factor rather than a change in kind. Owner decision OD3, accepted 2026-08-29; the eleven-circle burst cap and its own residual are owner decision 2026-09-08 option (a), and the TEN-circle account roster bound that puts the cap's deferral branch out of production reach is owner decision 2026-09-09 — both recorded on INV-W-445-EXPIRATION-WINDOW.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present per-circle timing as preventing a relay from linking your circles, must not limit that linkage to relays that carry SEVERAL of your circles (a relay holding one of them, plus an archive of another, is enough), and must not present the stagger as buying more than the NUMBER of distinct whole-second timestamps it produces — a number that is roster-dependent and falls to three at kMaxCirclesPerAccount — and in particular not as 'the archive-adversary defence', which it stopped being when the schedules were coalesced. Copy must equally not claim that a relay learns nothing about how many circles you are in, and must not scope that leak to a single carrier. There are three: the burst's connect-to-disconnect span at any relay that sees a burst (an inbox-only relay included); the same span on the PUBLISH POOL wherever that pool is COLLECTIVELY disconnected at teardown (the iOS-background burst and the Android foreground service); and the SIGNED kind-445 created_at deltas themselves, whose per-gap ceiling resolves the circle count exactly at five and six circles and to a PAIR or a TRIPLE otherwise - one bit coarser on those, never absent - and which persist in any archive of the events.

accepted_deviations.summary: Owner-directed reversal (recorded 2026-07-12, made public-by-default 2026-07-16) of Security Rule 10's no-public-profiles posture: the kind-0 + Blossom public profile module deliberately publishes the display name and photo, unconditionally, on save. Onboarding pre-fills an anonymous pseudonym and publishes it; there is no skip / pubkey-only path and no consent toggle. Its remaining boundaries are CI-enforced by check_profile_privacy_boundaries.sh.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not say a saved name or photo 'may be' published, must not imply a setting exists that keeps them private, and must not offer a circles-only name. Equally, this must not be described as a regression to be reverted.

accepted_deviations.summary: On iOS the SQLCipher DB keys use kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly rather than the library default kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked, so a background wake can open the database while the device is locked. Owner-approved to enable locked-device background location sharing.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim a locked phone protects Haven's data at rest. A still-powered-on device unlocked at least once since boot can have the OS surrender the DB key WHILE LOCKED; only a device powered off and not yet unlocked keeps it sealed. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this today — see docs/privacy/README.md, known gaps.

accepted_deviations.summary: Owner decision D8 (2026-08-28) accepts the iOS backup posture UNCHANGED now that circles.db carries the member directory — the payload change D5 said would deserve its own decision on its own timeline. The Haven data directory is getApplicationDocumentsDirectory() + '/haven' with no platform branch (haven/lib/src/services/data_directory_provider.dart:44-47), so on iOS circles.db, its -journal sidecar and session.sqlite sit in Documents/, the most-backed-up location the OS offers, and NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey appears NOWHERE in the tree — not in haven/ios/Runner/, not in any Dart or Rust path, not in a checked-in plugin. Android is unaffected: allowBackup="false" with no dataExtractionRules and no fullBackupContent (haven/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:48), so the posture is asymmetric and one-sided. What travels into a backup is ciphertext whose key is a ThisDeviceOnly Keychain item (see IOS-KEYCHAIN), so a restore onto a DIFFERENT device cannot open it; a SAME-DEVICE restore can, and reinstates a snapshot taken before a logout or a Delete Identity. wipe_all_mls_state deletes circles.db and session.sqlite with their sidecars and destroys both keyring entries (haven/rust_builder/src/api.rs:877, :983-986), but that destruction is DEVICE-LOCAL rather than absolute and no code Haven can write reaches into a backup to finish it.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that logging out or deleting your identity IRREVERSIBLY destroys the on-device member directory — nor anything else living in circles.db — because a same-device restore from an iOS backup can bring the encrypted file back. The claim that IS true is bounded: the deletion removes the file set from this device, and what a backup carries cannot be opened on a different device. Copy must equally not present the backup as harmless because it is encrypted — 'another device cannot read it' is the true half; 'a backup holds nothing of yours' is not. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this today. identityAdvancedDeleteBody stays inside the line by describing the act ('deletes your identity and all circle data from this phone') and asserting no permanence; the member-directory disclosure (owner decision D6) has had no surface since the Settings → Privacy page was removed on 2026-08-29, and no invariant carries status accepted_deviation against this entry yet; since that date a zero-disclosure accepted deviation is a permitted state (docs/privacy/README.md), so filing one is a deliberate act rather than an impossibility — the same holds for P4. INV-D-DIRECTORY-NEVER-LEAVES-SQLCIPHER stays 'enforced' and names this deviation in its statement and its note.

accepted_deviations.summary: The engine's stored convergence buffer has no per-group cap and no eviction API (upstream MDK #757, closed as not planned on 2026-10-01 with no fix). A Haven-side intake cap throttles ingest but cannot bound engine storage — an accepted insider-threat storage-DoS exposure.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim a circle member cannot consume unbounded device storage. Security Rule 12's backpressure bounds the FETCH, not the engine's buffer.

accepted_deviations.summary: kind-445 application messages carry a DETERMINISTIC NIP-40 expiration. The retired per-send design sampled it precisely to avoid a constant-TTL fingerprint identifying Haven clients among mixed MLS-over-Nostr traffic; group-level retention is what the protocol now offers, so the fingerprint is accepted. The send-side bound (RetentionBoundPeeler) BROADENED it, and that widening is accepted here too: the delta is no longer fixed at group creation, it is decided at SEND time, and Haven now stamps 228 s in circles it did not create — where it previously stamped nothing. So the discriminator is no longer only client-wide. In a circle whose declared message-retention.v1 window is absent, zero, or longer than 228 s, `expiration - created_at == 228` separates the Haven member's location updates from every other member's traffic on the same #h: a PER-MEMBER discriminator inside one group, sharper than the client-wide one because it attributes traffic within a group whose membership a relay cannot otherwise resolve. Accepted as the price of the two properties the bound buys — bounded relay residency, and location traffic not masquerading as membership traffic. A circle Haven created is unaffected: there every member stamps the same 228 s.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present the expiry as making Haven traffic less distinguishable. It does the opposite, in two ways: the constant is a client-wide discriminator visible to any relay or member, and inside a circle whose declared window is absent, zero, or longer than 228 s it is additionally a per-member one, because Haven's 228 s then differs from what that circle's other clients stamp (or from their stamping nothing); a circle declaring SHORTER is the one foreign case with no per-member split, since Haven stamps that declared value like every other client. Copy must also not imply the expiry follows the circle's own policy — Haven applies its own window whether or not the circle asked for one — and the value cannot be changed for circles that already exist.

accepted_deviations.summary: The corroboration gate deliberately keeps NO admin-side record of a departing member's intent, so there is no automatic admin-side backstop. The leave's intent is durable and the Android foreground service and WorkManager carry it on without the app being opened, so a crash no longer matters. Two cases stay unconverged: (1) at LEAVE_BOUND_MS (a day after the press) the leaver ends the leave on its own device whether or not any member committed it, and a last proposal for an epoch the circle has left is never committed; (2) the leaver's device takes no wake before the bound (switched off, or background sharing off with the app never opened again) while its SelfRemove was deferred or lost the order race. In either case no removal commit is produced and a stale roster ghost stays authorized until an admin manually removes it. SECURITY.md labels this 'Precisely-bounded residual (accepted)'.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not state that leaving always re-keys the circle within a bounded time. The automatically-unconverged case needs a manual admin removal and there is no admin-visible signal one is owed. NOTE: no user-facing string discloses this. The Privacy-page sentence that ASSERTED the bounded form ('usually within a few minutes') was removed with the page on 2026-08-29, so no shipped copy contradicts this record any more.

accepted_deviations.summary: The kind-30443 `d` slot id is a public, per-account coordinate every relay serving that account's KeyPackages can read. mint_d draws 32 bytes (64 hex chars), the width the Nostr transport binding fixes; builds before that fix drew 16 (32 hex chars), and THE BINDING MAKES THAT MALFORMED, NOT MERELY NARROW: `d` is 'exactly one tag, exactly one 64-character lowercase hex value decoding to 32 bytes', and 'if a required singleton tag is missing, repeated, has no value, or has extra values beyond the one defined here, the event is malformed' (transports/nostr.md), while foundation/key-packages.md requires an inviter to 'reject malformed or incompatible candidates before selecting one'. THE INVITABILITY COST IS NOW CLOSED, NOT ACCEPTED: a one-time, crash-safe retirement (decide_kp_slot_retirement, run by maintain_key_package ahead of the ordinary decision; sentinel kp_slot_retirement_done_v1) re-publishes the SAME tracked package into a freshly minted conformant slot and, only after a relay OK-ACKS it, publishes one NIP-09 kind-5 deletion of the orphaned coordinate ('a' = 30443:<pubkey>:<old d>, plus the observed id as 'e' and k=30443). Moving the same package rather than minting one keeps an in-flight Welcome against the retired coordinate decryptable, which holds for a tracked package whose lifetime is readable; an adopted slot (which holds no package) or a dead or unreadable package is replaced by fresh material instead, and the superseded material is deleted once the replacement is acked. The sentinel latches only on a completed migration, so a failed publish, an unacked retraction or an unanswered probe resumes instead of latching — and an unacked retraction does not consume the tick either, so a relay that never acks a kind-5 cannot starve rotation, republish-if-missing and heal behind it. WHAT REMAINS ACCEPTED is the historical residue: NIP-09 deletion is advisory ('relays SHOULD delete'), so a relay that ignores the request — or that was unreachable while the migration ran and comes back serving the old event — can keep the 32-hex coordinate publicly readable, and no client can force its removal. That residue is an era marker (which build of Haven first published the account), not key material: the value is CSPRNG-random and non-derived (never from an account key, MLS leaf key, KeyPackageRef or device label). A lenient peer that still selects the orphan is not stranded where the package was MOVED — it carries the same one this device holds — until that package is next rotated or reaches Lifetime.not_after, the spec's own deletion bounds; where it had to be minted, the orphan advertises material the account no longer tracks, so such a peer can fail to invite it. Proofs: haven/rust_builder/src/api.rs tc8_a_pre_fix_install_is_retired_onto_a_conformant_slot_via_real_ffi, tc9_a_conformant_install_is_never_retired_via_real_ffi, tc10_no_retraction_until_the_replacement_is_acked_via_real_ffi, tc11_an_already_published_replacement_is_adopted_via_real_ffi, tc12_a_conformant_account_scrubs_a_leftover_orphan_via_real_ffi, tc13_a_refused_retraction_leaves_the_migration_open_via_real_ffi, tc14_a_never_acked_retraction_does_not_starve_rotation_via_real_ffi, tc15_an_unreadable_row_is_retired_onto_fresh_material_via_real_ffi; slot shape pinned by haven-core/tests/kp_rotation_e2e.rs::a_first_publish_mints_a_binding_shaped_random_slot_id.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not present the slot id as carrying nothing a relay can use, and must not claim that retiring the old slot ERASES it: NIP-09 deletion is a request relays SHOULD honour, so an old 32-hex coordinate can stay publicly readable on a relay that ignores it, identifying which era of Haven first published the account. Copy must equally not claim that every Haven account is invitable by any Marmot client the moment it is installed — the retirement needs one tick with a reachable KeyPackage relay to complete, and an account with no reachable relay is unreachable for ordinary reasons anyway. The id is random and reveals no key material.

accepted_deviations.summary: With the Bluetooth mesh on, a device passes on to a circle's relays the location a fellow member sent by Bluetooth alone (member bridging, owner decision D-7, docs/BLUETOOTH_MESH_PLAN.md §5.5), so members far away can see someone who has no internet. The event is the sender's own, signed by its one-use key, so authorship stays hidden — but it reaches the relay tens of seconds after its created_at and off the bridging device's own publish rhythm. A relay of the circle, and any subscriber of the circle's routing id there, can infer that some member of that circle is offline and within radio reach of the bridging device's network address; when the sender reaches the same relay too, one event arriving from two connections links their two addresses. Bridging is on whenever mesh is on, with no separate switch.
accepted_deviations.forbidden_claim: Copy must not claim that turning the mesh on changes nothing a relay can learn, that a relay cannot tell an update was carried by another member's phone, or that a member without internet is invisible to the circle's relays. It MAY state that a passed-on update is the sender's own encrypted event, that the relay does not learn who sent it or what it says, and that the offline sender's network address never reaches the relay.

avatarPickerPhotoRemoved.reason: Snackbar confirming a photo removal that at least one profile relay acknowledged: the profile without the picture was published and the cached bytes were dropped. It is not a local-only action, and it does not say the removal reached every relay. Honest only because (1) the confirmation dialog (photoHeaderRemoveBody) precedes it and states that the hosted image survives, and (2) the sync status line on the same page never reads up to date while a relay the removal was sent to has not acknowledged it (INV-P-PHOTO-REMOVAL-IS-OWED-TO-EVERY-POOL-RELAY). On its own it must never read as a deletion promise, nor as removed from every relay. Its @description does not yet record this constraint.

changeNoticeKeepConfirmBody.reason: Consent step before the user releases a dropped removal's hold: it DISCLOSES exposure (anyone the user tried to remove who is still in the circle can see the location whenever Haven shares with it) and promises no protection. invariants.title: Only Best-profile iOS fixes ever become a published coordinate
invariants.statement: On iOS the session runs at one of exactly two accuracy tiers, and only a fix delivered under the Best profile — desiredAccuracy == kCLLocationAccuracyBest AND computed after the switch to it (the bestSince comparison) — is emitted to Dart, cached as the publish input, or returned as last-known. A kCLLocationAccuracyHundredMeters fix serves the stationary/movement detector and the freshness bound and nothing else; it never reaches a subscriber, the motion trigger or the relay. A live session holds that fix THREE times — the native lastBestFix, the location service's _lastStreamPosition, and the profile controller's anchor — and all three clear together, on stream cancel, on a toggle-off pause, on logout and on an observed access loss, so no full-precision coordinate outlives the session in any of them. The last-known read is age-bounded by the same freshness rule as the cache read, so the fix one rejects as stale is not served by the other. Emitting or caching a 100 m-tier fix, dropping the bestSince comparison, adding a third accuracy value, serving the native cache unbounded, or clearing fewer than all three copies, each falsifies this. That freshness rule is itself bounded in TIME. A coarse-tier confirmation may extend how long the Best anchor is served past its own timestamp, but never beyond kStationaryAnchorMaxAge (5 min), enforced in two places: IosProfileController escalates to Best at that age however many coarse fixes have confirmed the anchor, and _streamFixIsFresh refuses to serve a fix older than it whatever the confirmation says. A published location carries the instant of the PUBLISH and never the fix time, so without that cap a stationary backgrounded device would re-publish one anchor indefinitely and a peer would read "just now" for a coordinate hours old and up to 200 m wrong. Removing either half of the cap, or measuring it from the confirmation rather than from the anchor's own timestamp, falsifies this too.

invariants.title: On Android a reboot restarts the publishing foreground service with no user action
invariants.statement: RebootReceiver is android:enabled="true" and ForegroundTaskOptions sets autoRunOnBoot:true, so the location-publishing foreground service comes back by itself after a reboot; and the exception stops there, because RestartReceiver stays android:enabled="false" so an OS/OEM kill is never auto-restarted. invariants.title: A circle that can no longer send is detected and named as that circle, and no background burst creates one
invariants.statement: Two halves, each falsifiable on its own. (a) A BACKGROUND burst never publishes a removal-bearing auto-commit — a departing peer's eviction, the only commit a receive path stages: a burst makes no such commit at all. It receives in the mode that makes no commit (`Lifecycle::receives`): the eviction comes due in the engine and stays due, so nothing is staged and there is nothing to publish, to park or to roll back, and no burst opens a publish-before-apply window the OS may end mid-flight. A location sent in the mode that makes no commit is not sealed while an eviction is due AND the leave it answers still stands unconsumed at the circle's epoch — it is answered deferred, typed (`SendHeld::DepartureDue`; `SessionManager::departure_holds_a_send`) — and the engine's own commit such a hold stages anyway is undone in that hold. The engine's timer alone holds nothing: MDK keeps it in memory and does not drop it when another member's eviction is applied, so once that commit has consumed the leave the next background send seals, at the new epoch and not for the member who left. A plane's advance in the mode that makes no commit is the engine's inputs-only one, which runs none of its maintenance: no eviction is staged there, and a leave the engine mints again is recorded for a full drive to send. The hold on commits is the newest live plane's to set — a plane let go late cannot lower the hold of the burst that replaced it — and it does NOT cover another isolate with its own `CircleManager` over the same database. A burst and a pause leave the eviction due. The first full drive in a claimed foreground makes it, under a record (`SessionManager::evictions_left_due`) — unless another member's eviction is applied first, after which nobody here makes one. A fanout is the only way a commit leaves the device: every commit is staged under a durable fanout record written in the lock hold that staged it (`SessionManager::stage_commits`) — in the full mode only, which the live plane takes while its session's lifecycle is `Foreground` (`Lifecycle::receives`), a lifecycle a session enters on its caller's claim and on nothing the core infers (`live_sync::Claim`), and a bridge entry while its caller's claim stands (`Claimed`); an event in hand when that lifecycle ends is taken in as it began, and the full advance it leaves owing is not made once the engine is had after the foreground has ended, so it stages nothing behind the pause — it is sent by the fanout driver alone, the bridge's plain publish refusing every kind 445, and it is rolled back only by the fanout driver, on the proven refusal of every relay the record was frozen for and only while none was ever possibly exposed. The one other rollback happens before anything was sent, in the lock hold that staged the commit, and on any plane: a commit any call stages beside a recorded pending commit a relay may hold is unstaged there (`SessionManager::unstaged_beside_a_fanout`), and so is one staged in staging mode whose record could not be written or whose circle is still waiting out a refusal, and one a failed full advance left staged with no record, whose change stays queued. A commit that could be neither recorded nor rolled back in its hold is not published and is owed to nobody: it stays staged, unsent, its circle is told (`ChangeNote::ChangeUnrecorded`), and the rollback is tried again at the next hold that stages; whether it was rolled back is read from the engine's state and never from the rollback call's result, so a rewind that landed and then errored is a rollback. None of these is a drop: the engine re-arms the eviction; after a rollback by the driver Haven stages it again only after a wait that starts at one minute and doubles to an hour and is kept with the circle across sessions, and the wait holds on every hold that can stage it. A location send inside the wait is not made at all: what the circle has received is settled by the engine's inputs-only advance, which stages nothing, and while the wait still runs and the engine still announces the eviction the send is answered deferred without the engine being asked to send (`SessionManager::departure_holds_a_send`), so nothing is staged only to be undone. The holds that cannot avoid the engine's preflight — a staging-mode hold, a leave, the three admin-policy sends (hand-over, step-down, the epoch-rotation repair), a plane's inputs-only advance — undo in that hold an eviction the engine stages inside the wait, handed to nobody and owed nowhere (`SessionManager::unstaged_beside_a_fanout`). While that wait runs this device shares nothing to that circle — one minute up to an hour per refusal — and, once the eviction is due, nothing is sealed at the epoch the member who left can read; when the wait is over a full drive itself gives the circle the engine's full advance, which stages the eviction again under a record (`SessionManager::evictions_left_due`) — as it does for an eviction a burst or a pause left due, with nothing arriving —, and a full drive that finds the wait still running says when it ends, so the live plane's drive task wakes for it then (`SessionManager::restage_due_after_ms`); and a removal the driver undid is recorded for its circle (`ChangeNote::RemovalUndone`), written durably while the stored record still says the commit was rolled back and before that record is deleted, by whichever pass finishes the rollback — the drive, the session's next engine call, or the pass before the next open; a note that cannot be written keeps the record, and the engine held, until it can, and the note is kept until it is acknowledged. The sweep every wake runs (`run_catchup_all_circles`) drives in the finish-only mode and makes no commit; the sweep that stages and drives in full (`run_catchup_in_foreground`) is reached by no entry point of the app, and the driver's poll entry and its location-send entry (`Publishing::ingest_for_poll`, `Publishing::seal_location`) only by the bridge's `*_driven` entries. Every drive is given a mode by its caller, and there is no default (`DriveMode`): the full one, for a caller whose claim that the app's lifecycle reads `resumed` stands, and a finish-only one, which the live plane takes in a background burst and in a session only started. A process with no live plane — the Android service's isolate among them — drives in the mode its caller's word gives (`Claimed`), and the Android service passes no claim. The finish-only mode sends the frozen bytes of a pending commit a relay MAY ALREADY HOLD — one acknowledged it, an attempt may have exposed it, or one was begun and never returned — to each relay that was attempted before and is due, and stores each answer. It BEGINS nothing and undoes no record: no rollback of a record, no bound, no record for a new commit, no full advance, no queued change, no Welcome, no publish of anything that has no record, no first transmission — a record no relay may hold is not taken up, and within one that is, a relay never attempted is not attempted —, no call without a whole row's budget left. Five things it does do besides sending. It confirms a pending commit whose STORED record holds a relay's acknowledgement — one its own call has just stored, or one an earlier call stored, with no relay called again — when the wake has a whole fold's budget left and the commit does not change its circle's relays: that change is a full drive's to confirm — applied away from a claimed foreground it would hold its circle's sends until one (`ChangeNote::AwaitsForeground`), and the full drive applies it without that hold — and a record whose intent cannot be read is taken for one. A confirm it cannot begin for want of that budget is left, the call asking to be driven again, and a send meanwhile is told what holds it (`SendHeld::Acknowledged`: a commit a relay has acknowledged, awaiting its confirm). What is left of a record it confirmed — the relays still owed, its Welcomes, its end — is a full drive's. It finishes a confirm whose transaction an earlier call landed and whose engine half then failed, through the engine's own confirm — its replay of what was parked, and an inputs-only fold of what that hands back; nothing is decided by it, the commit being already applied and on record. Where that commit changed the circle's relays it is finished only once the circle is durably marked as waiting for the foreground (`ChangeNote::AwaitsForeground`), which holds the circle's sends for every call that is not a claimed foreground's — a burst's, a paused session's, and one in a session that has only been started — answered deferred, typed (`SendHeld::AwaitsForeground`), until a full drive has COMPLETED in a claimed foreground: the mark is cleared at that drive's end, for each circle with the engine held and the lifecycle asked again, so a pause that lands while the drive waits ends nothing. Finished, the device seals at the new epoch for the new relays while its subscriptions are still on the set the app last gave it, so it would miss a later removal and seal for whoever was removed. It writes the one record nothing else would keep, for a leave the engine has minted again. It undoes, through the engine's `publish_failed`, a commit it finds staged with NO record — one handed to nobody, and the one thing it undoes. And it retires a queued change of the group, its circle told first, at the moment that change is what holds the circle at its epoch. When what it retires is a REMOVAL of somebody the circle still lists, who it named is kept first — member ids, at rest in the SQLCipher-encrypted circle store and nowhere else, never in a log, a panic or an error — beside the note that says a removal was dropped (`ChangeNote::QueuedRemovalDropped`); and while one of them is still listed nothing is sealed for the circle by any call, a claimed foreground's included (decision 238; `SendHeld::RemovalUnmade`), so neither the device unattended nor its user in front of it goes on sealing for the member the admin asked to remove. That hold ends when nobody the removal named is listed any more — a member any commit this device applied took out stops holding, and with the last of them the note is taken back, since what was asked for is so (somebody removed the member, or they left); the names are kept while branch selection could still withdraw that commit, which brings them back with the hold and the note, and are then dropped — or when the note is acknowledged, which deletes the names with it; they are deleted with the circle too. It never ends at a drive. The live plane is the plane that drives a stored record unasked (`Lifecycle::drives`): in the full mode in the foreground; in the finish-only mode in a background burst, from its open to the pause that ends it, and in a session that has only been started, whose start asks for that one drive and which arms no timer for another (the drive timer is armed in the foreground and inside a burst only); and not at all while paused. A drive outside the foreground rides the session's own drive pool like any other, and begins a relay call only with a whole row's budget left. That state is entered only on a caller's claim that the app's lifecycle state reads `resumed`, carried by the call (`live_sync::Claim`) and made in exactly one way: the bridge turns the `foreground` flag of the entry it was called by into the claim (`foreground_claim`), and the Dart layer fills that flag from one strict read — the app's lifecycle state is `resumed` (`appIsResumed`) — which answers no for a state that has not been set, for `inactive`, `hidden`, `paused` and `detached`, and where there is no binding. On Android `resumed` is the activity resumed AND its window focused: a Haven window that is visible but unfocused (split-screen, freeform), or under the notification shade or a system dialog, reads `inactive` for as long as that lasts. Three entries take the claim, and a session's START is not one of them: a start runs for seconds — a connect wait, the open-time advance of every circle, every REQ — and a claim read when it was asked would be acted on after the app may have left, so a start always leaves its session only started. The three: the claim itself (`claim_foreground`: no REQ is touched and no relay is waited for; a session it puts in the foreground is served as one, once — a drive of the stored records is asked for — and a claim that promotes nothing does nothing), which the app's service makes from a fresh read the moment its start holds the engine and the heal makes again after every `resumed` event; a foreground open (the app's resume, the user's own repair, the health tick's whole-session re-anchor), which is refused outright without the claim; and the health tick, which without the claim changes no lifecycle, asks for no drive, re-issues only the REQ of each repair key that is due — the endpoints that went quiet, and with them a relay-closed inbox key due at that instant — and where the whole-session repair was due says so (`HealthAction::AwaitingForeground`) instead of reporting a health it did not find. The core still cannot see the screen: the claim is the only proof it has, and what makes it trustworthy is that it is made from that one read and from nowhere else, and that the lifecycle's writers are callable from the session alone in a shipped build. A pause the app issues while `NostrSubscriptionService.start()` is in flight waits for that start, its claim included, and then pauses the session it produced. A stop ENDS the start: the engine's stop is issued at once on the handle the start has built, the start adopts nothing while a stop is in flight, a start whose engine is not built yet starts nothing once it is, a session that came up across the stop is stopped again, never adopted and never claimed for, and a stop that lands while the start is making its claim stops the session that start had adopted; in each case the start fails as ended by a stop, a type of its own (`SubscriptionStartEnded`), so nothing takes a running set from it and nothing counts it as a restart that failed. A second start, and a second stop, join the one in flight. Nor does a start issued BEHIND a pause bring a session up where that pause stopped the engine. There is one `start()` in the app, in `LiveSyncResubscriber._fullRestart`, and it reads whether a session is wanted immediately before the start and again after it (`MapShell.liveSyncWanted`, computed from the lifecycle the binding reports at that instant: not while it reads `detached`, and not while it reads `paused` on a branch whose pause stops the engine — Android always, iOS with background sharing off). So a heal that had not yet reached `start()`, a full restart between its own stop and its start, and a delta that falls back to a full restart all start nothing, and a session the answer changed under is stopped again; the heal timer is never armed while the app is away: it is cancelled by a pause, by a detach and at dispose; a heal that completes behind that cancel arms nothing; and it is armed only by a `resumed` dispatch and, at a mount, only if the app reads `resumed` at that instant (`LiveSyncHealBackstop`) — a process the operating system relaunched in the background mounts under `detached`, `inactive` or `paused` and arms none there — and only a restart that was attempted and failed lengthens its interval — a start the user's own pause ended, and a restart declined because no session was wanted, do not. On iOS with background sharing on the pause keeps its session — that process is the background receiver — and a start issued there from the background is not refused: the one made on purpose, where the consent that makes this process the receiver resolves after a pause that had read it off and stopped the engine, is ordered behind that pause's stop however long the stop takes — joining the stop the pause issued, never issuing one, so a consent that flaps on a pause that kept its session stops and starts nothing — with the burst, or the idle close, that pauses its session chained behind it (`MapShell.healBehindStop`) — only ever started, never in the foreground, because the claim is the strict read and that process is not resumed. A session that dies there between bursts is not started again by a timer: no heal timer is armed there. The next burst finds none on the typed lifecycle, or finds it gone at its open, which answers no session typed (`BurstOpenFfi::NoSession`), and starts one directly into itself (decision 190, `startSessionIntoBurst`) where a live session is wanted, once the consent has loaded; a burst that cannot start one publishes nothing and reports a failed open to the sharing-health model (the existing lost-subscription fault). What is NOT proved: `MapShell`'s pause and resume handlers themselves are not mounted host-side, so which of these each branch reaches, and that each handler stops after every await once a later pause or resume has been dispatched — a count of those two dispatches taken at the handler's entry, not a read of the lifecycle, so a pause the user has returned from releases and announces nothing even where the window has since lost focus — is pinned from the source and exercised only on the device lanes. A session nobody has claimed for is not in the foreground, and no number of unclaimed ticks puts it there; neither is a background burst or a pause. A session only started makes no commit and records nothing: its open-time advance of every circle, made before any REQ, is the inputs-only one, and what it receives and a send are taken in the mode that makes no commit; a burst and a pause make no commit and record nothing; and what a started session or a burst drives, it drives in the finish-only mode. A drive runs on a task of its own, off the ingest worker, through a publish pool that carries the driver's sends and nobody else's; a pass under way when the foreground ends reads finish-only from that moment and stays so whatever the lifecycle becomes — its leash only narrows, and one taken outside the foreground never reads full at all (`live_sync::drive::Leash`). A pass belongs to the stretch of the lifecycle it began in: once that has changed — the foreground ended, a burst was paused, a started session was claimed — it takes no further relay and has no budget left for anything it had not begun (`ModeSource::stands`), a confirm of a stored acknowledgement included. What the engine was already ASKED for runs to its end: a confirm under way when the foreground ended completes with its fold, which can record a commit and end the record; and a publish of something that has no record, already handed to its publisher, runs out that publisher's own retries (three attempts, forty-nine seconds at most). From the flip it decides nothing new, and does nothing it had decided and not begun — a pass reads its mode, decides, and then waits for the engine, for as long as whatever holds it takes, so each act that may not outlive its lifecycle is asked for again with the engine held (`relay::fanout::Still`): a rollback, the bound, a confirm, a Welcome's hand-over and a full advance decided before that wait are not made once the lifecycle has changed in it, and the record stays as it is stored; a send, a leave and an ingest are made in the mode that makes no commit, and a send a due departure holds in that mode is held —: it takes no further relay — one it was still waiting for is given back uncalled — for a recorded event or through its publisher of what has none; a relay it already held is not used for a first transmission, so nothing is marked as begun for a commit no relay has been sent (one a relay may already hold is sent again to a relay already held that was attempted before, as the finish-only mode sends it); it makes no queued change, begins no publish, confirms nothing, rolls nothing back and applies no bound; and a proposal a hold hands back after the flip is not kept for a later foreground. It stores the answers of the calls it has out, and an acknowledgement among them is confirmed by the next pass that begins — a burst's, a started session's or the foreground's — without a relay being called. A background burst opened over such a pass does not wait for it; the pause that follows waits for what that pass has out before it cuts the radio, and a stop gives the call up — it is then stored as possibly exposed, and nothing is rolled back for it. (b) A circle MDK's persisted `unrecoverable` flag says can no longer send is read as such on every circle read and after every restart (`CircleEngineState::Unrecoverable`, `RecoveryCause::Unrecoverable`), reads live again once an authenticated rejoin repairs it, and is announced as its OWN per-circle `LiveSyncEvent::GroupUnrecoverable` refresh nudge naming the pseudonymous `nostr_group_id` and never the MLS group id, crossing the FFI as the additive nullable `unrecoverableNostrGroupId`. event_kinds.note: The eviction auto-commit is a kind-445 control message (h tag, no expiration), built by the rev-pinned peeler. This invariant is about WHEN it is put on the wire: never from a background burst, always from a foreground pass, and never abandoned. A parked commit is a 445 this device owes and has not sent.
