invariants.title: A relay is sent a recorded commit or proposal again only on one schedule per relay, and a commit it may hold asks for no wake of its own after a day
invariants.statement: An event under a durable fanout record — a commit or a bare proposal — is sent to a relay again only when that relay's schedule says so, and the schedule is per RELAY across every record that owes it: after an unanswered call MDK's thirty seconds doubling to an hour, after a relay that could not be reached five seconds three times and then the same doubling, after `rate-limited` one minute doubling to an hour. What failed at a relay before it last acknowledged something is not counted against it, so a record kept after it ended does not lengthen another record's wait there. A stored attempt that lies ahead of the clock — the clock was stepped back — is not read by the relay's schedule (`relay_due`): its own record is due at once and is stamped again by that one call, and no OTHER record is made due by it. A relay another send holds for the whole of the driver's five-second wait is not attempted: nothing is stored or counted for it, the drive asks to be run again five seconds later — on the live plane its drive task makes that run then, in the foreground and, while one lasts, in a background burst; a session only started arms no timer, and nowhere else does anything schedule it: the caller's next call makes it — and the relay's own wait is as it was, however many times that happens. A relay a record still owes that is being called for ANOTHER record is not tried either, and a drive that could not try a relay it owed never asks whether the record's day is over; a drive in which no relay was due does ask. A drive that finds nothing due makes no call and takes no relay. On the live plane a drive runs when something was staged, wherever a caller claims the foreground — the claim made behind a session start in a resumed app, the heal's claim for a session started before it, a foreground open, a health tick that carries the claim —, once at a session's start and once at a background burst's open — each in the finish-only mode, which makes no first transmission (a record no relay may hold is not sent, and a relay never attempted is not attempted) and calls a relay only when it is due — and, in the foreground and inside a burst only, when the time its last drive reported has come (never sooner than five seconds, and not at all when it reported none), and never because an event arrived or a relay came back — save the one network return below: an inbound storm, a flapping connection, repeated foreground opens, a background burst and a started session between them, a fresh session for every visit to the app and that timer add drives, not calls — the schedule is the stored record's, so it is carried from one session to the next. A COMMIT's first drive makes one call outside the schedule, once, to the soonest of its relays; a proposal's does not, and when a relay's wait is over its one call goes, within ONE circle, to a commit's record before a proposal's (read from `SessionManager::stored_fanouts`; the cited test proves the cross-circle half only), and across circles to the record the relay was called for least recently — a commit one circle cannot get a relay to take never keeps another circle's leave from it. A proposal's record ends, making no further call, once nothing can act on its event: its circle has left the epoch it was proposed for, or this device's copy of the circle is marked removed. A commit every relay refused that the engine stages again by itself — the eviction of a member who left — is staged again only after a wait of one minute doubling to an hour, kept with the circle across sessions and holding on every hold that can stage it: a location send inside it is not made at all, and a leave, the admin-policy sends and the full advances undo in their hold what the engine stages there. When the wait is over a drive in the full mode stages it again itself, at the first full drive at or after the wait's end; a full drive that finds a wait still running reports what is left of it (never under five seconds), so the live plane's drive task wakes then and a foreground device stages on the wait's own minutes — the original and five more in the first hour (minutes 1, 3, 7, 15, 31), then 63, 123 and hourly. For every other path, and for a device that is not in the foreground, that is a ceiling. What a relay that goes on refusing is sent is a NEW commit event each time, under the same routing tag, three frames each inside the relay client. From a day after it was staged — for a record the open wrote, a day after that open — a pending commit a relay may hold is sent to a relay at most once an hour and reports no time to be woken at for that relay's sake — its drive still reports five seconds when a relay that was due could not be had, and zero when its wake was cut short —: it rides wakes the app has for other reasons, so a relay that accepts the socket and answers nothing is not handed a timetable of where the device is. Every such call dials its relay, and a record keeps the relays it was frozen for: a relay that is dead, or that a later change took off the circle's list, is dialled on that schedule until the record that owes it ends — for an applied commit, two relays holding it or a day after the later of its staging and its first acknowledged attempt (each relay having answered one attempt); for a pending commit known to remove nobody and never possibly exposed, a day after its staging, when it is undone; for a proposal, two relays holding it, a day, or nothing being able to act on it any more; and without limit for a pending commit a relay may hold, or one that removes a member. This adds no connection plane: every such call is made on a publish pool INV-R-PUBLISH-POOL-NO-KEEPALIVE already names. Pacing a relay per record, calling a relay that is backing off for any record but a commit on its first drive — the device coming back on a network (`wake_unreachable`, called on the live plane only when a relay dropping while live left the whole pool, as it stood then, with no relay up and a relay then came back — never on a pause's termination — at most once a minute on the driver's clock, in the foreground or a burst only, and then making only the relays that could not be reached due) and a stored attempt further ahead of the clock than the longest wait are the two stated exceptions —, calling a relay because an event arrived, a relay reconnected, a burst opened or the app came to the foreground, a session only started sleeping on a drive's hint, a finish-only drive making a first transmission, publishing an owed commit no relay acknowledged again inside its wait, sending a leave again after its circle has left the epoch it was proposed for or after this device was removed from the circle, calling it because some other record ended, staging a refused eviction again in each new session, or scheduling a wake for a day-old commit a relay may hold, falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: A commit or a standalone proposal re-sent byte for byte from its durable fanout record: same kind, same id, same tags as its first send.

invariants.residual: Scoped to events under a fanout record, which the app stages and drives through the live plane while its session's lifecycle is `Foreground`, entered on a caller's claim alone. That plane's drive task sleeps on the time its last drive reported (`EngineProcessor::drive_due_again`: never less than five seconds, nothing on a report of zero, nothing outside the foreground), so a relay that is due is called when its schedule allows, and a refused eviction is staged again when its wait ends; the timer adds a drive, never a call. A session start claims nothing and asks for no drive; the claim made behind it in a resumed app asks for one: with nothing due that drive reads the store, takes no relay and dials nothing. No other plane has one: the driver's poll and send entries, which nothing in the app calls yet, drive only their circle's pending commit when they are called — a circle with none costs a read of the store and no relay is called for it — and a relay that never answers is called on the same one schedule whatever sends, polls or drives. A drive in the finish-only mode makes no record's first call and begins none without a whole row's budget left. A stored re-staging wait that lies further ahead of the clock than the longest wait is treated as over, so a clock stepped back costs one early staging rather than an eviction held for days. While a stored attempt lies ahead of a stepped-back clock, the calls it stands for are not counted, so the relay's wait for other records is SHORTER than its full history would make it until the clock passes that instant. Nothing bounds how often a commit can find its relay held by another send for longer than the five seconds it waits: the relay's gate serves waiters in the order they came, but a call that gives up gives up its place, so such a commit is sent LATER than the schedule says, with no limit set here. A proposal's record that has stopped being useful is deleted only once its going changes no relay's wait; until then it is kept, making no call, with no bound of its own: it goes once the records that still count calls at its relays have ended or been acknowledged. And a leave is still sent, on the schedule, for as long as its circle stays at the epoch it was proposed for: up to a day to a relay that answers nothing.

invariants.title: A circle that fell behind walks only its own history, at a bounded pace
invariants.statement: When the epoch-stall detector arms (eight distinct undecryptable kind-445s at one stalled epoch, or a want of room), the circle owes ONE walk of its own history, asked by its own routing id at the relays its traffic was sent to - the #h the live REQ already names, so no relay learns anything new - and nothing account-wide. It arms at most once per stalled epoch, then re-arms at most once an hour while the circle stays at that epoch, and only on a claimed foreground's ingest - except that a walk which brought back something it could not take in re-arms at once (MDK parity), its next walk paced by the refused range's doubling waits; the walk runs only inside sweeps the app already makes or the live plane's RefetchOwed, so it adds no timer, wake, task or REQ shape. Reading a peer's message at the circle's current epoch ends the run's evidence but keeps that pacing, so a minted flood cannot buy a walk per peer message. The circle reads Stalled only on three walks the relays answered in full that brought back nothing that moved it - never on a count of arms - and Stalled triggers no automatic action. Residual (OI-4, accepted): a flood into a circle with no peer message read for two hours or more (three fruitless walks, an hour's pacing apart) can make it read Stalled.

invariants.title: No relay-delivered event is acted on unless its id and its signature verify
invariants.statement: Every EVENT frame the relay pool would otherwise hand on, from every relay, passes Haven's own check before the pool stores it, de-duplicates it by id or notifies anything of it: the VerifiedEvents admission policy calls Event::verify(), which recomputes the id from the event's parsed fields AND checks the signature over that id, and refuses anything else without a log line or a reason. A genuine event a relay spells differently on the wire (key order, an extra field, escapes) verifies as itself. The relay pool's own verification is skipped for an event whose claimed id it has already verified (nostr-relay-pool 0.44.3, SharedState::verify_and_cache), so without the policy a relay that holds no key can have any author, kind, content, tags or timestamp accepted under an id the client has seen: a forged copy of the user's own profile merged into the one Haven signs, a forged relay list that redirects an invitation, a forged own KeyPackage that makes Haven sign a deletion of another of the account's events, a forged copy of a group message that takes the genuine one's place in every id-keyed memory so the device loses a commit. The policy only runs on a client built with it, so verified_client is the one place a relay client is built in shipped code (RelayManager::new and build_engine_client call it), and it gives the client no gossip store, which the SDK would feed before asking the policy. MDK's relay client, which the durable fanout publishes through, builds no client of its own and verifies nothing itself: RelayManager::fanout_transport hands it the publish client, so what a relay sends back on those sockets passes the same policy. Handing it any other client falsifies this, as would an MDK release whose relay client built a client, installed a gossip store, an admission policy or a signer; its source is re-read by a test on every run. Naming a Client or RelayPool construction in any other source file of haven-core, the FFI crate or the soak rig (test witnesses are marked, in listed files, inside test modules), removing the policy from the constructor or installing a second one, replacing verify() with verify_signature() or verify_id(), or moving the check to after the pool's id-keyed de-duplication falsifies this. State a relay could have planted before the check existed does not outlive this release's storage reset, which deletes every store that could hold it. It does not promise delivery or freshness: a relay can still withhold, can still serve an older genuine replaceable event where it is asked alone, and a relay that forges is neither banned nor reported.

invariants.title: An invitation is sent again only to its invitee's inbox relays, on a bounded schedule, for one day
invariants.statement: On the driver's invite entry (which the app's invite into a circle uses since W9n), an invite's Welcome is sent only once its commit is applied, from its hand-over (the first full drive that settles the confirmed commit), and each Welcome a circle is founded with from the record its create writes before returning; either is sent only to the invitee's kind-10050 inbox relays that pass the foreign-relay filter (never their NIP-65 list, never the inviter's own inbox), as the same stored bytes every time, one relay at a time no sooner than 30 seconds after the last attempt with the wait doubling to an hour, until one inbox relay acknowledges it, and for no longer than a day from the hand-over or an hour before a Haven invitee's 96-hour inbox window would lose the backdated wrap, whichever is sooner, never past its KeyPackage's not_after, and never once its invitee is off the roster or this device's copy of the circle is removed or disbanded; until the hand-over an invite's route is kept only in the encrypted circle store (table welcome_routes). The bridge's plain publish entry refuses every gift wrap, so no Welcome leaves but from its record. A founding Welcome outstanding with no record is never sent. Sending it to any other relay, before its commit is applied, after an acknowledgement, after its end or after it stopped being wanted falsifies this.

invariants.title: No location is sealed for a circle while a commit it fetched waits unread
invariants.statement: While a circle holds a current-epoch commit this device fetched and has not taken in -- a commit the catch-up pager held back from a page, by event id, from the moment it is held until an ingest on any plane takes that event in, or a live REQ's stored replay, until it is taken in -- the driver seals no location for that circle: the send is deferred, typed, as stored input owed to the circle, and nothing fetched is dropped. No pass that completes without the commit ends the hold, and a relay left out of its REQ's coverage sends no stored replay, so it never holds a seal. Such a commit may remove a member, who would read a location sealed at the epoch before it. Sealing a location for the circle in that window falsifies this.

invariants.title: A disbanded circle is sent nothing and asked of no relay
invariants.statement: Once an admin has disbanded a circle -- read from MDK's durable tombstone every time, so a crash that lost the announcement changes nothing -- this device seals no location for it and no receive plane or sweep asks a relay for its routing id, while its other circles carry on. Sealing for it, or a REQ for its routing id, falsifies this.

invariants.title: Backgrounded on iOS, presence is revealed only at publish instants
invariants.statement: While backgrounded on iOS with background sharing ON, from the completion of the pause branch's teardown until the next burst's open, the live-sync engine holds no standing subscription and no socket IT ASKED FOR: pause_subscriptions CLOSEs every REQ, sweeps any that a partial unsubscribe_all left registered (both bounded by RELAY_LIFECYCLE_OP_TIMEOUT and log-and-proceed on expiry), drains what is already downloaded through the Pause marker (note_delivery_gap, never a forget_*, so an un-applied hold-back survives; best-effort — on a dead worker or an unacked marker the router is cleared directly and the undrained backlog is re-downloaded by the next re-anchor), waits UNCAPPED for every in-flight publish (Security Rule 13) — a drive of stored fanout records under way when the pause began counts as one for its whole pass, whether it began in the foreground or in the burst the pause ends: from the moment its lifecycle changes it begins nothing, and what it had decided and not begun is not done — the decision is read again with the engine held — it takes no further relay, for a recorded event or through its publisher, makes no first send, and begins no confirm of a stored acknowledgement — while what the engine was already asked for runs to its end: a confirm under way completes with its fold — a foreground's can record a commit and end the record, and hands over no Welcome once the foreground has ended; a burst's applies an acknowledged commit and settles what was received, and stages, records and hands over nothing — and a publish of something that has no record, already handed to its publisher, runs out that publisher's own retries (three attempts, forty-nine seconds at most). A pass is given two rows' budget, sixty-two seconds from when it began, and one that only finishes begins a relay call only with a whole row's budget — thirty-one seconds — left. So what is waited for is what that pass has out: one call of MDK's relay client, twenty seconds at most, when it was sending a record; the rest of a confirm's fold or of a publisher's retries when the flip found it inside one — and only then terminates every relay through terminate_all_relays (client.disconnect(), re-read and re-asserted over RELAY_TERMINATE_ROUNDS rounds, never client.shutdown()) and closes the session's own drive pool (RelayManager::shutdown, on a pool nothing else publishes through), so that where the termination converges the crate's per-relay connection task and its 55 s pinger exit with it — see exception (iii) for where it does not. Each publish tick runs exactly one bounded burst instead: open_background_burst re-issues every REQ in the Resubscribe phase — each circle at its persisted cursor less GROUP_RESUBSCRIBE_BUFFER_SECS, and the inbox at INBOX_RESUBSCRIBE_LOOKBACK_SECS on every INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ-th background burst, never the cold-start window — asks for one drive of the stored fanout records in the finish-only mode, on the session's own drive pool — a relay a pending commit's record was frozen for is called only when a relay may already hold that commit (one acknowledged it, an attempt may have exposed it, or one was begun and never returned), this relay was attempted before, and its schedule says it is due, with the same bytes; a record whose every attempt found its relay unreachable, and a relay never attempted, get no first transmission from a burst —, waits up to BURST_BACKLOG_WAIT_SECS per (relay, subscription) endpoint for EOSE so a peer commit ingested here is APPLIED before the location is encrypted, publishes, folds due KeyPackage/relay-list maintenance onto the warm publish pool, settles (COMMIT_SETTLE_WINDOW_SECS from the last commit activity, capped by BURST_SETTLE_CAP_SECS, which bounds idle follow-on activity only and never an in-flight publish), pauses, drains any commit-critical publish still on the shared publish pool, and shuts that pool. A pause that drives no burst — nothing eligible, or a publish still inside kLocationPublishOverlapGuard — runs that same teardown on its own (closeIdle, on the same chain and under the same in-burst flag, so it can never run beside a burst), which is what makes the gap before the first burst no exception. THREE exception classes and one separate plane, all stated. (i) The teardown STOPS wherever the foreground reclaimed the engine, leaving the publish pool to the next pause's teardown. (ii) An engine start still in flight when the pause runs — a cold launch's, or any return's that the user left again within seconds — does not outlive it. On the branches whose pause STOPS the engine (Android; iOS with background sharing off) that stop is the pause's first act — on Android with background sharing on it is issued ahead of the two platform writes that hand publishing to the foreground service, and each of those is guarded, so a write that is slow or throws costs the service a prompt start and never the stop — and it ends that start: the engine's stop is issued at once on the handle the start has built, so the start fails at its next check instead of running out its connect wait, open-time advance and subscribe ladder; a start whose engine is not built yet starts nothing once it is; a session that came up across the stop is stopped again, never adopted and never claimed for; and a stop that lands while the start is making its claim stops the session that start had adopted, and the start then fails as ended by a stop instead of returning over a stopped engine (NostrSubscriptionService; its tests park a start and issue the stop meanwhile). On this branch the pause's `pauseSubscriptions` WAITS for the start — the engine's pause takes the lock the start holds and can end nothing early — and then pauses the session it produced; such a session was claimed for only if the lifecycle still read `resumed` when the start held its engine. A start issued BEHIND the pause brings no session up where the pause stopped the engine: the app's one `start()` (`LiveSyncResubscriber._fullRestart`) reads `MapShell.liveSyncWanted` immediately before and after it — a heal that had not yet reached `start()`, a full restart between its own stop and its start and a delta that falls back to one all start nothing — and the heal timer is never armed while the app is away: it is cancelled by a pause, by a detach and at dispose; a heal that completes behind that cancel arms nothing; and it is armed only by a `resumed` dispatch and, at a mount, only if the app reads `resumed` at that instant (`LiveSyncHealBackstop`) — a process the operating system relaunched in the background mounts under `detached`, `inactive` or `paused` and arms none there, so none ticks behind a pause. (The `resumed` dispatch the framework synthesises on the way out of its `detached` seed is the one exception, and the statement ends on it.) On THIS branch a start issued behind the pause is not refused — this process is the receiver — and two things follow. The one start made from the background on purpose, where the consent that makes this process the receiver resolves after a pause that had read it off and stopped the engine, is ordered behind that pause's stop however long the stop takes, and the burst, or the idle close, that pauses the session it produces is chained behind the start (`MapShell.healBehindStop`); that edge joins the stop the pause issued and issues none of its own, so on a pause that kept its session a consent that flaps stops nothing and starts nothing. And a heal that reaches `start()` only after the pause's teardown has run — a cold launch backgrounded before its first start was issued — brings up a session that is only started and holds its REQs until the next burst's teardown pauses it, which is for as long as nothing is publish-eligible, when no burst comes. A session that DIES between bursts is not started again by a timer: none is armed there. The next burst finds none on the typed lifecycle, or finds it gone at its open, which answers no session typed (`BurstOpenFfi::NoSession`), and starts one directly into itself (decision 190, `startSessionIntoBurst`) where a live session is wanted, once the consent has loaded, then waits out the backlog and pauses as any burst; one that cannot start it publishes nothing (nothing is sealed before a receive has run) and reports a failed open to the sharing-health model. What remains is two waits. On this branch, until that start has returned, claim included, the engine holds the REQs it issued: a connect wait of up to five seconds, the open-time advance, the subscribe ladder and, where the app was resumed when the start held its engine, a claim, which waits for no relay: what an earlier pass left owed is published by the session's drive task, which a pause ends at the commit in flight. On every branch, a stop asked for before the start has built its engine waits for the engine factory: an identity read and the MLS database's open, which in a foregrounded app can itself wait up to twenty seconds for the Android foreground service to release the session. A start that fails is cleaned up by the start, not by the pause. (iii) The termination is a REPAIR PLUS A WATCH, never a prevention: nostr-relay-pool's own retry loop can re-open a REAL socket over the pause's Terminated and hold it with 55 s pings indefinitely (the race is inside the pinned crate, between two adjacent statements of InnerRelay::disconnect, so the engine cannot make it impossible), and non-convergence after RELAY_TERMINATE_ROUNDS warns with a COUNT only. What is promised instead is that no such socket SURVIVES — run_monitor's radio-off watch cuts every one, including the strand this loop cannot see at all (a Disconnected write that landed BEFORE the pool's Terminated store), and unrequested_connections is how many there were. The publish pool is a separate plane the burst does not own — the motion trigger may re-open it between bursts — and how it closes SPLITS BY PLANE, so no single claim covers all three. On this branch and on the Android foreground service it is closed COLLECTIVELY: RelayManager::shutdown is one client.disconnect() over the whole pool, reached from every burst teardown here (_shutdownPublishPool) and at step 9b of every Android delivery cycle plus onDestroy — so on BOTH background planes a relay carrying exactly one circle in a pass sees connect-at-its-own-publish through disconnect-at-teardown, a tail that grows with the circles published after it and converges over the CSPRNG permutation to the whole pass length. Only in the FOREGROUND is there no collective disconnect: publish_relay_options() is ping(false).reconnect(false).sleep_when_idle(true).idle_timeout(10 s) polled once a minute, so each relay's socket sleeps independently in (60 s, 70 s] after that relay's own last send. Presence is revealed to a circle relay at every burst instant. Since PUB-COALESCE one burst publishes EVERY publish-eligible circle, so for an eligible circle the REQ/CLOSE pair and this device's kind-445 for that circle now coincide on essentially every burst — the fractional mismatch this clause used to disclose is gone for that class. A burst's drive adds one contact of its own: a relay a pending commit was frozen for — the circle's relays as they were when the commit was staged, which after a change of relays may no longer be the circle's — sees a connection from the drive pool and that commit's event again at a burst instant, on the record's schedule (thirty seconds doubling to an hour; from a day after it was staged at most once an hour), until a relay acknowledges it and the burst confirms it. Three things that sentence leaves out. A relay that could not be reached is tried again after five seconds, three times, before its wait starts doubling, and one that answered `rate-limited` from a minute: a burst that lasts long enough can dial a dead relay up to three times, the drive timer running inside a burst. The event is byte-identical each time, so a relay that keeps what it is sent can link the address the device had when it first sent the commit with the one it has now. And a session that has only been started — in a backgrounded process, where a start was issued behind a pause — makes that contact once, at its start, and holds no standing one: it arms no drive timer. A wake adds a second request of its own, for what the engine refused — in the sweep every wake runs, and in the redelivery a burst runs when the engine refuses something during it: the ids of objects it had no room for or let go — the events a hand-back of stranded input could not give it included — are asked for by id, at most two REQs of up to 128 ids to each of the circle's relays a sweep, and past 1024 owed ids the circle's history as a range, a page budget a sweep. The range's ceiling is never lowered: a pass that halts carries a walk down from it — below a full page dated entirely in one second, too, keeping the range owed, since events beyond a relay's page limit that share one second are unreachable by NIP-01 paging — and the walk ends the range only when it has reached the circle's start, every relay answering in full in the pass that reached the start (a relay unreachable during an earlier pass of the walk is covered by the same assumption the cursor makes), with the engine holding something of every event any pass of it brought back, one it recorded and then erred on included — an event the engine had no room for, erred on with no record of its own, or was never asked about is on record nowhere else, so such a walk begins again at the ceiling. An id a sweep could not discharge is asked for again after a minute, doubling to once a day — eleven requests in its first day, one a day after — and nothing but a verdict, or every relay asked answering a request that names it with no event at all, ends it: no count of tries and no count of epochs. An answer that brought some of the ids it was asked for proves nothing about the rest — a relay may clamp a request's limit and send a subset — and those are asked for again by themselves, out of the same two REQs. Ids are asked for from the front of a queue an id rejoins at the back each time it is asked for, so nobody who mints ids keeps theirs ahead of one that was owed first. A new epoch of its circle makes every owed id and the owed range due at once, and the owed ids are then asked for: by the sweep in which the epoch moved, out of that sweep's same two REQs and before its next round of advances for the circle (the first two moves of a sweep; the range at the circle's turn); on the live plane, which holds no REQ of its own to ask with, by a status the app answers with one refetch — the redelivery above — at most once a minute, and which the plane does not wait for, so there a refused event can still be overtaken. When the engine has no room for anything a request brought back, the ids already asked for wait at least as long as the soonest of those just asked, and an id not yet asked for keeps its turn; the range keeps a schedule of its own — a pass that carries its walk down leaves the rest due at once, and one that carries it no further (halted where it began, or come to the bottom with something still owed) doubles the wait before the next — and is asked for when due whatever the ids beside it are waiting for. THE WORST CASE, to each relay of the circle. For ONE owed id: one REQ naming it at each time it is due — eleven on its first day, one a day after — and one more at each new epoch of its circle. For a FULL ledger, 1024 ids and a range: two REQs of 128 ids a sweep and no more, so four sweeps to ask for every id once and, with no new epoch, eight REQs a day once the waits have reached a day; for the range, one pass of at most eight pages of 500 events for each routing id the circle keeps when it is due — every sweep, and every minute on the live plane, while a walk of it is descending; and when a walk reaches the bottom with something still owed (an outsider's events a relay goes on serving and the engine goes on refusing), one such descent a wait, the wait a minute doubling to a day — a descent as long as the circle's history on that relay, which an outsider who keeps the engine's store full can lengthen. A new epoch brings those forward and adds none: the sweep it moves in still sends two REQs of ids and makes one range pass; on the live plane a member who commits as often as they like has a full ledger asked for, and its range walked eight pages further for each routing id the circle keeps, at most once a minute. Somebody outside the circle can fill the ledger and cannot move an epoch. Nothing here opens a connection, holds a REQ open, or adds a request to a wake beyond those. A location record a process died with is deleted by the next drive with no relay contacted: nothing sends a location again. A leave's proposal goes to the relays its record froze when the engine minted it — one proposal per epoch the circle reaches — by any drive that runs anyway, a background one included, on the same per-relay schedule as a commit's record, until enough relays hold it or a day has passed since that proposal was minted; it holds no REQ and arms no timer, and once the leave has ended on this device (the copy found removed, or a day after the first press) nothing of it is sent again. Anyone who knows a circle's routing tag can make it owe such ids, so the schedule, not the count, is what a relay is spared. Four classes still produce a re-anchored #h REQ with no kind-445 for the circle it re-anchored: (a) the burst publishes NOTHING when openBurstPublishWindow returns null (no identity, disclosure not accepted, location permission revoked, one-shot GPS timeout) or consent flips inside the pass — the open precedes the publish unconditionally; (b) a circle in the stored live set that is not publish-eligible is re-anchored on every burst and never published to at all. The two sides are read from different places, and the subscription side is a STORED SNAPSHOT: resume_burst re-anchors active.group_subs, which subscribe_circle and unsubscribe_circle mutate off a circlesProvider emission and the session's own routing follow mutates by itself — at every burst open, at every start, and whenever any plane moves a circle's row. So the subscribed set is every ACCEPTED circle AS OF THE LAST FOREGROUND EMISSION (groupsForCircles), each listed where its row now routes, while the publish target is re-read FRESH at seal time (Publishing::seal_location -> get_circle -> circle.relays, frozen into the location's record) and filterPublishEligibleCircles additionally excludes quarantined and engine-flagged Unrecoverable circles, so this is a permanent mismatch rather than a fractional one; (c) a per-circle send that fails or is DEFERRED by the MLS engine, and the tail of a roster past kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11), which the burst itself defers to the next tick; (d) a circle-set change applied DURING the background window — a circle the user REMOVED while backgrounded is left by the follow its leave wakes, but one dropped from the roster any other way keeps its #h REQ re-anchored until the next foreground emission. A RELAY-SET or routing-id change applied while backgrounded no longer splits the pair: the session follows the row at the burst open, and listens at the relays the circle left for a day, so for that day the old relays see a REQ with no kind-445 of this device's behind it. Coalescing also LENGTHENS the exposure it narrows: the burst holds its connection across the whole staggered publish pass, so the connect-to-disconnect span grows with the number of eligible circles — saturating at the cap — and is a single-relay estimator of that count for every relay in the union resume_burst connects, inbox relays included (PUB-COALESCE). An inbox-only relay sees the same pair on every INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ-th burst with no kind-445 to pair it with, which is itself the inference that this pubkey is background-sharing now. The three RELAY-CONTACTING Dart maintenance timers — KeyPackage, relay-list, and the 15-minute subscription-health tick — are foreground-only on this branch EXCEPT BEHIND A SYNTHESISED `resumed`: all five of the scheduler's arming and firing gates read the looser predicate, which differs from the strict one only where no state is set, and on a device one always is (the binding reads the embedder's seed, or the message that replaced it, when it is initialised); but the `resumed` the framework synthesises on the way out of that seed reads `resumed` while it is dispatched, so the resume handler's maintenance re-arm — on iOS inside that dispatch — passes the arming gates, and where the launch settles at `inactive` the KeyPackage and relay-list ticks, gated at arming only, fire and contact their relays (see the paragraph that ends this statement). (suspendForBackground cancels all three at the pause; health is gated again where it fires — and carries, from the strict `resumed` read, the claim without which the core changes no lifecycle, asks for no drive and makes no whole-session re-anchor —, the other two at arming only), because the burst IS the repair, at 72-168 s rather than 15 min. The FOURTH timer is not: the ~45 min public-profile anti-entropy sweep keeps its armed timer, gates at FIRE time (_appIsForegrounded) and RE-ARMS itself on the backgrounded branch, so it is a periodic CPU-only wake between bursts that contacts no relay. The complementary arm: every OTHER pause STOPS the engine rather than pausing it (MapShell.shouldStopLiveSyncOnPause = !(isIOS && backgroundSharingEnabled)), including iOS with background sharing off, and the Android foreground service shuts its own publish pool at the end of every cycle. NOT COVERED, and open: a process the operating system launched in the background — everything above is about a process that was PAUSED. On a device the lifecycle is never unset — both embedders seed it `detached` — but the binding reads it once, when `main()` initialises it, and a message the engine receives before then replaces the seed with no dispatch; a later one is dispatched, every state on the way synthesised (`resumed` first out of `detached`), to the observers registered at that instant, and `main()` awaits its start-up work before `runApp`, so the shell is normally not yet one of them. A shell therefore mounts under whatever the binding already reads, and its handlers run only for changes after the mount. Whatever it mounts under, the mount arms its publish scheduler, motion trigger, ownership heartbeat and hourly prune. Its start-up (MapShell._runStartupTasks) contacts relays only if the app reads `resumed` when it runs: otherwise the pool pre-warm, the KeyPackage publisher, a one-shot location publish to every circle where the location disclosure was accepted, the flag-off pollers and, five seconds later, a public-profile refresh and a retry of any own-profile publish left queued are owed to the first resume — inside the resume's 30 s debounce too — which runs them once, and a pause landing while that contact opens its pool stops the rest of it and owes it again (ForegroundStartUpGate); carrying on the leaves this device asked for is part of that contact and reads the lifecycle again before each circle, so a pause stops it at the next circle (a call already under way runs to its end), and a burst, the Android foreground service or a WorkManager wake carries the rest on, claiming no foreground. What the start-up runs regardless reads a gate of its own: the maintenance timers arm only in front, and the live-sync heal starts a session only where one is wanted. Mounted under `detached`: no session is wanted and no heal timer is armed; the first message after the mount is then dispatched `resumed` first, so the resume handler runs with nobody looking — it opens the location cache, arms the foreground timers and the heal timer, re-arms the maintenance timers, attempts a publish, runs the KeyPackage publisher and a profile refresh, and starts a session, which is not claimed for (the claim is read when the start holds its engine, and the lifecycle no longer reads `resumed` by then) — and pays what the start-up owed. Where that message is `paused` the pause handler runs right behind it, in the same dispatch, and everything above applies — with the residual already stated for this branch: the start can reach the engine after the pause's teardown has run, and the session then stands until the next burst's teardown. Where it is `inactive` no pause runs: the session holds as in the next case, the heal timer ticks beside it, and the KeyPackage and relay-list ticks fire and contact their relays. Mounted under `inactive` (neither the Android nor the iOS embedder sends `hidden`, so no binding rests on it at a mount there): the mount starts a session — unclaimed, staging nothing, arming no drive timer and no heal timer — that holds its group and inbox REQs and their sockets for as long as the process stays there, and the start-up's relay contact waits for the first resume; nothing pauses the session while the process stays there, and its publishes are not bursts; if the app leaves `inactive` for the background, `paused` is dispatched and the pause handler runs then (iOS sends `inactive` from `viewWillAppear` whatever follows). Mounted under `paused`: the shell takes the pause it was never dispatched (`pausedAtMount`) — it stamps no foreground and, once the background-sharing consent has loaded, or 5 s after the iOS session arm began if the platform has not answered it, the consent then still reading off (read earlier, the pause would take the branch of sharing off), runs the pause handler unless a lifecycle change has reached it since — so every branch's pause applies: on Android the heartbeat is cancelled and, with sharing on, the session handed to the foreground service; on iOS with sharing on the burst plane is installed and pauses what the start-up starts, at the next burst's teardown; with sharing off no session is started. The start-up's relay contact is owed to the first resume. THE `inactive` cases are open, on two axes only a device can settle: what the binding reads when the shell mounts, and where the launch settles. Closing them — starting a session only for a `resumed` that is not the synthesised one, or routing an iOS background launch with sharing on through the pause branch — waits on an owner decision. The dispatch order this paragraph rests on is pinned host-side; that the seed is `detached`, and that the engine replaces it until the binding first reads it, are read from the Flutter engine and framework source, not tested. A burst's NIP-77 pass (INV-R-NEG-ADVERTISES-NOTHING) runs on that drive pool before the seal, so every session it opens ends with the pool's close at the pause; e2e-ios-background-publish's P2c reads the drive pool's connected-relay count (LiveSyncFfi::drive_pool_connected_relays, which throws rather than answer for a session without one) and requires zero on its first answer after a burst.

The Rule-13 link — the in-flight publish gauge before the radio cut — is pinned twice: rule13_a_burst_never_pauses_with_a_pending_publish_outstanding asserts the source order in BOTH pause_subscriptions and resume_burst's failure exit (and that neither cuts through a bare client.disconnect()), and pause_never_disconnects_while_an_auto_commit_awaits_its_ok proves it over a relay withholding a real OK. The drain-before-clear link has two oracles (pause_subscriptions_drains_the_intake_before_it_clears_the_router, a_pause_marker_drains_every_queued_event_before_the_router_is_cleared). invariants.title: One standing connection lets a relay link identity to circle membership
invariants.statement: While the app is FOREGROUNDED, a single persistent socket per relay carries both the inbox filter naming the user's own pubkey (gift-wrap #p) and every subscribed circle's routing-tag filter (#h), so a relay serving both planes can correlate identity to circle membership by connection continuity — the ephemeral per-message 445 author keys do not prevent this. The overlap remains the default configuration for a circle created before the 2026-10-31 relay-plane change, whose relays were the invitees' inbox union — on a default install the same three seed relays as the user's own inbox — and a circle another client created carries whatever relays its creator chose. A circle Haven creates without named relays shares no relay with its creator's own Inbox, KeyPackage or Profile lists (INV-R-CIRCLE-RELAYS-FROM-LOCATION-POOL) and avoids every invitee's inbox and NIP-65 relays unless too few other pool entries are left; the join returns for it only when a member's lists name one of its relays — a user who later adds it to their own inbox (the exclusion is applied at create, never retroactively), an invitee the pick had to fill from, or a member added later, for whom nothing is re-picked. For CIRCLE relays the standing form is now foreground-only: backgrounded on iOS with sharing on the two filters ride ONE BOUNDED BURST PER PUBLISH TICK and the join is per-burst rather than continuous, and every other pause stops the engine outright. Per-burst is not per-publish, but since PUB-COALESCE it is much closer to it: a burst re-anchors EVERY circle's #h REQ, connects the whole relay union, AND publishes every publish-eligible circle, so for an eligible circle the join now coincides with that circle's own kind-445 on essentially every burst. It stays strictly wider in three cases — a burst whose publish window refuses publishes nothing at all; a subscribed circle that is not publish-eligible (quarantined because its encrypted state failed to load, or engine-flagged Unrecoverable) is re-anchored on every burst and never publishes; a deferred or failed send, and the tail of a roster past kMaxCirclesPerBurst, re-anchors without a kind-445 — and the join is no longer instantaneous: the connection is held across the coalesced publish pass, whose length grows with the number of eligible circles and is therefore itself a single-relay estimator of that count. That is a narrowing, NOT a strict one: an inbox-ONLY relay — one holding the user's kind-10050 inbox but none of their circles, an independent set — carries no kind-445 to correlate with, and where it used to see one continuous socket it now sees a REQ/CLOSE pair every 72-168 s (the 120 s nominal cadence, jittered ±40 %), which is itself the inference that this pubkey is background-sharing right now. Raising INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ removes that cadence at the cost of background invitation latency (OD4-b, accepted, not yet raised); at the shipped value the inference is disclosed rather than mitigated. Both planes still open from the same address in the same seconds, so the two-socket join by source address is unchanged. In the foreground a third socket can join them: the session's drive pool dials a circle's relay to send a commit or a leave it has recorded — an event that carries that circle's routing tag — from the same address, and sleeps about a minute after its last send as every publish pool does; and, only while its pass is in the full mode, it dials an invitee's inbox relays to deliver a Welcome an applied invite released, and a circle's relays for a proposal no record could be written for. After the foreground has ended it begins no call for a record that was never sent, and takes no further relay; a publish of something with no record that was already under way runs out its own retries.

event_kinds.note: The inbox-plane filter side of the correlation: a #p filter naming the reader's own pubkey. Standing while foregrounded; backgrounded on iOS it rides every INBOX_BURSTS_PER_REQ-th publish burst, which is the residual cadence an inbox-only relay reads.

The group-plane filter side: an #h filter naming each subscribed circle's routing tag. Standing while on screen; on iOS-bg one bounded burst per publish tick — every burst re-anchors every circle AND publishes every publish-eligible one, so the join coincides with this circle's own kind-445 on essentially every burst, and the burst's connection is held across the whole staggered pass.

invariants.title: Timing and size metadata stay visible; jitter narrows it but padding does not exist
invariants.statement: The publish cadence is jittered uniformly over [nominal*(1-0.4), nominal*(1+0.4)] = [72 s, 168 s] from a CSPRNG, which defeats short-window rhythm fingerprinting but not long-run averaging; message sizes are NOT padded, so location updates fall in a narrow, recognisable size band. Narrowing the Rust spread without the Dart endpoints, or presenting the jitter as defeating traffic analysis, falsifies this.

invariants.title: One burst publishes every eligible circle; only the CSPRNG stagger keeps their created_at stamps apart, and how much it buys shrinks with the roster
invariants.statement: Circles publish in ONE jittered burst per interval — up to kMaxCirclesPerBurst (11) of them, the rest deferred to the next tick, a branch kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) keeps out of production reach — with consecutive encrypts at least kPublishStaggerMinGap (2 s) apart, so no two circles share a kind-445 created_at. The per-gap CEILING is kPublishStaggerMaxGap (9 s) only for small bursts: PublishStagger.maxGapFor prices each gap at the burst's own size, so it shrinks to 3333 ms at kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10) — the largest burst a bounded roster produces — and to a flat 3 s one circle further on, at the cap. The per-circle schedules this invariant used to enforce are gone, and so is the claim they carried: every relay carrying ANY of your circles now sees the same burst rhythm, so relays each holding only ONE of your circles can match the timing and tell those circles belong to the same phone. Two costs the record did not previously carry, both stated here rather than in the deviation alone. FIRST, the surviving archive claim is NARROWER than 'the stagger is the archive-adversary defence': after coalescing the archive reader gets the link anyway, from the shared inter-burst interval sequence. What the stagger still buys is ROSTER-SCOPED, because the observer reads no milliseconds — only floor(created_at) — so its alphabet is the whole-second delta, and maxGapFor thins that alphabet monotonically as the burst grows: {2..9} (eight values) at n <= 4, {2..6} at n = 6, {2..5} at n = 8, and {2,3,4} at n = kMaxCirclesPerAccount (10), the largest burst a bounded roster produces; {2,3} is maxGapFor's answer one circle further on and no observer reaches it while the bound holds. Both production call sites price the gap at the real burst size — the foreground tick through sampleGaps(count), the background pass through sampleGap(totalPublishes: total) where total is _encrypted.length + pending.length. COALESCING CAUSED THE THINNING: pre-P5 every gap was priced at the default totalPublishes = 2, so the alphabet was always eight. At small rosters the downgrade in KIND is real — a byte-identical created_at is a zero-cost equality join over a whole-network index (created_at_A == created_at_B, decisive on a single burst), while eight admissible offsets force a windowed correlation that must first hypothesise WHICH two circles share a device and then test that against a sequence of offsets. AT THE ROSTER BOUND IT BARELY IS: a three-element alphabet is three shifted equality joins over that same whole-network index, still un-targeted mass linkage, so what survives at ten circles is a constant factor rather than a change in kind. SECOND, coalescing makes the NUMBER of circles you are in a SINGLE-RELAY observable. Backgrounded on iOS the burst's engine socket connects the WHOLE relay union — every circle's relays AND the inbox relays (relay_union) — at the open and disconnects at the pause after the staggered pass, so the connect-to-disconnect span grows by one stagger gap per additional eligible circle (mean 5.5 s while the per-gap ceiling is the full 9 s, narrowing toward 2.5 s as the burst approaches the cap, the pass bounded by kPublishStaggerMaxSpread = 30 s) and is measurable server-side by ANY relay in that union: one carrying a single circle of yours, or an inbox relay carrying none of them. Sharply: the old scheme leaked the circle count only as a RATE, to shared relays that already read it off the multiplexed #h filter; the new one leaks it as a DURATION, to relays that previously could not know it at all. The account bound caps that estimator at ten, one circle under where the per-gap ceiling saturates. Since 2026-10-31 each circle Haven creates gets its own three relays from the eight-entry location pool, none of them an inbox relay, so a device in several such circles holds a wider union than when every default circle rode the inbox's seed relays: more operators can read that duration estimator, and circles on disjoint relay sets — the case PUB-COALESCE's cost (1) links by their shared rhythm — become the common case. Restoring per-circle schedules is not the fix and is not proposed (it never decorrelated anything at a shared relay, and cost one radio wake per circle per interval); what falsifies THIS entry is a burst that publishes two circles inside one whole second, a stagger drawn from anything but a CSPRNG, or a per-gap floor at or below one second. SCOPE NOTE (Bluetooth mesh, opt-in): one send falls outside the burst's rhythm altogether — a fellow member's location passed on to the circle's relays behind this device's own send (member bridging). It is another member's event, its created_at tens of seconds older than the send, and it is no part of the stagger; what a relay reads from it is INV-R-MESH-BRIDGE-TELLS-A-RELAY-A-MEMBER-IS-NEARBY-AND-OFFLINE.

invariants.title: Every server Haven contacts observes the device IP
invariants.statement: Haven ships no Tor, proxy or onion transport, so each relay it publishes to or reads from, the map tile provider, and whatever host a co-member chose for their profile picture all observe the device's IP address on every request — including the eight profile relays and six discovery relays the user did not choose and cannot remove, and the three relays Haven picks from its eight-entry location pool for each circle it creates, which the user does not choose either and cannot change in the app. Any copy implying network-level unlinkability, anonymity or IP hiding is false.

invariants.title: The eight profile relays never overlap the six discovery relays, the eight location relays overlap neither, and the user cannot remove them
invariants.statement: PRODUCTION_PROFILE_RELAYS (8) and PRODUCTION_DISCOVERY_RELAYS (6) are disjoint by construction and disjoint from the account seed defaults, and both are contacted unconditionally even when every relay the user chose is private; the curated eight cannot be taken out of the profile group at EITHER layer — Settings offers no remove control on a curated Profile row (matched across URL spelling variants, so a case or trailing-slash difference cannot bring the control back), and usable_profile_relays() unions the defaults back in on every resolution, so a row deleted by any other route still leaves the relay dialled. PRODUCTION_LOCATION_RELAYS (8) is host-disjoint from the account seed, the discovery plane and the profile pool, each of its entries is on its own registrable domain, and it is not user-chosen either: no Settings category lists it and nothing in the app edits it, and Haven itself dials a pool entry only as a relay of a circle it was picked for. The profile pool also shares no operator with the account seed any more: wss://nostr.mom, run by nos.lol's operator, was retired on 2026-10-31 (RETIRED_PROFILE_RELAYS) — an operator overlap is recorded at vetting, which no test can check. The copy must therefore keep saying "that you do not choose". Resizing either pool without updating the paragraph that spells both counts fails the copy tie.

No such path exists: all relay traffic goes through the nostr-sdk WebSocket client and all HTTP through package:http, both of which use the platform stack, and LocationMessage carries no address field.

The no-IP-in-payload half is covered by the LocationMessage field tests cited here; the no-bypass half rests on the current dependency set alone.

invariants.title: Global passive observation and a compromised device are out of scope
invariants.statement: Haven's design makes no claim against an adversary who can watch many relays simultaneously, nor against an adversary who controls the user's own device; no mixing, cover traffic, padding or remote-wipe mechanism exists, so removing this disclosure would leave the reader to assume coverage the code does not provide.

invariants.title: The Nostr secret key stays in OS-protected storage
invariants.statement: The 32-byte identity secret is persisted only in flutter_secure_storage (Keychain / Keystore), is read back per use rather than held, and no code path serializes it into a Nostr event, an HTTP body or a log line; this becomes false the moment a secret-bytes value is bound to a long-lived field or interpolated into any outbound payload.

invariants.title: No key material reaches a log, print or Debug rendering

At runtime the key-material floor (tooling/e2e/ci/scan-logs-for-secrets.sh) runs unconditionally inside tooling/e2e/ci/scan-logs.sh, before the identifier scanner and on every sink the wrapper is handed, so each wrapper citation below is a citation of that floor.

invariants.title: No identifier of any shape reaches a log
invariants.statement: Nothing that could tell one user, circle or device apart from another — a pubkey or npub, an MLS or Nostr group id, an event id, a KeyPackage slot, a subscription id, a relay URL or host (the default pool included), an IP, a circle/display name or petname, a coordinate or geohash, an absolute epoch, an exact count of circles/members/relays/events, an absolute publish/receive instant, or remote-authored prose — is interpolated into a log, print or panic call in haven-core, rust_builder, haven/lib, the haven/integration_test harness or the Tier-1 soak rig under tooling/soak (src AND tests), in any build, encoding or truncation; where a line must say 'the same circle/peer/relay as that other line' it renders a per-process salted alias handle, magnitudes are bucketed and instants are relative. Each of those trees is scanned as its own root with its own floor, so a collapse in one cannot be masked by volume in another; the rig is the one root where the blessed-wrapper rule does NOT apply, because its tags must be deterministic for its determinism test to mean anything while log_alias handles are salted per process — so it mints its own ordinals through functions named outside that vocabulary (sim_tag, sim_magnitude) and emits tags disjoint from production's (simdev#, simcircle#, simrelay#, simevt# against circle#, peer#, event#, relay#), which matters because both land in the same evidence file from the same process. This becomes false the first time such a value, or a prefix of one, or an unreviewed {:?} rendering of one, reaches a log call — in Rust, Dart, Kotlin or Swift — and the first time the rig renders a haven_core, cgka, nostr or openmls value through the Debug format family, whose impls print a real MLS group id and absolute epochs.

invariants.title: Every captured E2E log is scanned for key material and declared identifiers before it is echoed or uploaded
invariants.statement: On every lane that captures a device, simulator or test log — the Android and iOS core-flow lanes, the profile, integration, relay-customization and background-catchup lanes, the seven Android scenario lanes, the three iOS scenario lanes, and the unit-test transcripts of rust-check.yml's six cargo jobs and coverage.yml's rust-coverage (cargo llvm-cov) and flutter jobs — every captured log (the logcat, the unified-log exports, the full and final-attempt drive transcripts, the relay logs, the host diagnostics, the wire-proxy log, the redacted wire summary and the tee'd test transcripts) passes through tooling/e2e/ci/scan-logs.sh, which runs the key-material floor (scan-logs-for-secrets.sh) AND the runtime identifier scanner (haven-logscan) before any of it is echoed into the job log or handed to an upload step: on the two recording lanes against the manifest sealed from the identifiers the run declared over the proxy's control channel plus the host needles; on every proxy-less device lane against the host needles alone (the harness's fixed seeds derived to pubkeys, the role coordinates, the canary constants and the lane's own injected values, sealed with no declared Dart plant because no channel could hand the app one); and rules-only over the unit-test transcripts, which mint nothing declarable, with the summary saying so. The Tier-1 soak lane is scanned the same way and TWICE, because neither manifest subsumes the other: once against the manifest the rig sealed from its own declarations (the device keys, group ids, relay URLs and coordinates it minted in process, which nothing outside it could declare) and once through the same host-profile gate every proxy-less lane uses, which adds the harness's fixed host needles and the lane's endpoint exemptions; both run inside tooling/e2e/ci/run-soak-core.sh, before the workflow's upload step, and a leak there deletes the whole evidence tree and leaves one harness-authored line in its place so the upload publishes the fact of containment rather than the evidence. Two captures are REDUCED on the way in rather than scanned whole, because their raw form is legitimately full of what Rule 15 forbids uploading and no sink class could forgive it: a platform `dumpsys package` dump is filtered to the `android.permission.…` lines the lane actually reads (logscan_permission_extract, the three Android permission lanes), and a third-party Blossom server's access log — the server's own view of its client, carrying blob digests, the uploading pubkey and the base64 kind-24242 auth header — never becomes a file at all, only a count of HTTP methods, no-method lines and error keywords (logscan_http_log_summary, the Android profile lane). Both reductions are then scanned as `diag` sinks like every other file, so their safety is checked and not merely asserted. A leak (rc 1) deletes every scanned sink before the failure-artifact upload can see it, and the gate fails closed — an absent or non-executable scanner binary, a declaration sidecar a recording lane's drive never wrote, a missed positive control, an unmet line or declaration floor is a red lane, never a skipped scan. This becomes false the first time a captured log reaches an upload-artifact path or a `cat` without having passed scan-logs.sh, the first time a lane scans a capture with the bare floor instead of the wrapper, the first time --rules-only is used over a device or drive log, the first time a leak verdict leaves a sink on disk, the first time either reduction is bypassed and the raw platform dump or the raw third-party access log is kept, or the first time an absent binary, sidecar or manifest lets a scanning step exit 0.

invariants.title: The needle declaration sidecars and the sealed manifest never leave the runner
invariants.statement: The declaration sidecars (*.needles.decl), the sealed needle manifest (*.needles.json) and the wire-canary manifest (*.canaries.json) under /tmp/haven-soak/needles/ hold the run's declared identifiers verbatim — pubkeys, group ids, event ids, names, coordinates, and the digests of secret-class values — and never leave the runner: their directory is a constant with no environment override, the manifest is written 0600 into a 0700 directory and never overwritten, no workflow names one of them or their directory in an upload-artifact path, a step summary, an issue or PR body, or a cat/tee/head/tail/base64 command in a workflow or a lane runner, the scanner and its wrapper print counts, classes, encodings, rule ids and sink:line only (the manifest by basename), and every lane that records or seals — the two recording lanes and every proxy-less lane that runs the scanner — rotates the directory before its first capture and removes all three shapes in a final always() step after its last upload. This becomes false the first time one of those files (or a wholesale /tmp upload) appears in an upload path, the first time a workflow or runner reads one of them into a job log, the first time the scanner's value-disclosing local triage flag appears in a workflow, the first time a recording or sealing lane lacks the pre-capture rotation or the final discard, or the first time a sidecar from one run is still on the runner when the next run's proxy starts.

invariants.title: Release builds log nothing from any isolate

invariants.title: Circle encryption keys are not the identity key
invariants.statement: The MLS leaf signature key of every circle differs from the Nostr identity key, and the identity key is never used to sign a kind-445 group message; this becomes false if a group's credential is minted from the identity keypair or if the identity signer is handed to the group-message builder.

invariants.title: Losing the phone loses the identity
invariants.statement: There is no escrow, no server-side backup and no recovery flow: the secret exists only in the device keystore, so the only recovery path is a user-made nsec backup. This becomes false the moment any code path uploads or shares the secret for recovery.
invariants.residual: Nothing fails if a key-escrow or cloud-backup path is added: the guarantee rests on INV-K-SECRET-KEY-NEVER-LEAVES-DEVICE's log/commit guards, which detect logging and committed secrets but not a deliberate upload. No test asserts the absence of a recovery endpoint. Nor is the fact disclosed: onboarding's warning (onboardingCreateIdentityWarning, 'If you lose this phone or delete the app, your identity is gone') was removed at the owner's direction on 2026-11-04, and the only remaining mention is the backup sentence in the delete-identity confirmation (identityAdvancedDeleteBody), which a user meets only when deleting.

invariants.title: Delete Identity clears the device and nothing else
invariants.statement: deleteIdentity destroys the Rust identity, the secure-storage entry, the SQLCipher circle state, every SharedPreferences key on the reviewed delete path and the encrypted tile cache — and issues no unpublish for anything already on a relay or on the Blossom host. No live-sync engine is left up by it: the engine is stopped before the wipes and again behind the circle service's one-way latch, after which nothing can open the database to start one — the shell that owns the engine's restarts stays mounted across a logout, so a restart queued behind the first stop could otherwise build a new engine during the wipes and leave its REQs, the inbox one among them, standing on the deleted identity. Where the engine answers that stop as still holding, or does not answer it within the one restart budget both stops share (65 s in all), the wipe proceeds all the same — removing the key comes first, and a user who kills the app during an unbounded wait would keep it. A stop given up on is torn down on the Dart side at once — its session delivers nothing more, and no session is adopted until the engine's stop returns — and the engine's stop is bounded: it waits one relay operation for its lifecycle lock and then tears down beside a holder that will not let go, so that core's REQs are closed and its relays told to close within about seventy seconds whether or not it answers drained — a connection task the stop's bounded termination timed out on keeps its socket, with no REQ, until the process exits; its open handles on files the wipe has unlinked last until its last task ends, at worst until the process ends. The next identity signed in to in the same process is handed nothing that was built from this one: every such provider — the relay-preferences handle and the three relay lists, the circle list, the invitation and KeyPackage providers, the location service with its in-memory cache and its cached pubkey, the schedulers and the per-identity state notifiers (`identityScopedProviders`) — is dropped at the end of the logout and again at the login, and the event router reads its circle service at each event, so the next identity's inbox REQ is issued on its own relay list and its Welcomes reach its own store; the logout's end also clears the clock-skew detector's evidence (this identity's peers' pubkeys and clock offsets), which nothing of this identity refills behind the reset because a wiped location service records no sample; the event router keeps no wedge verdict of its own, because MDK persists a circle's halt in the database the wipe deletes. It then shuts the publish pool — after every stop has returned or been given up on, after the wipe and after the key is deleted — so the next identity's first publish opens sockets of its own and never rides this identity's, which would link the two at that relay (the Dart side's location, commit, KeyPackage and relay-list publishes all ride that pool, RelayManagerFfi's own manager; a pool still being opened is waited for and shut too). No publish of this identity can start on the pool by then — every publish needs an MLS operation the latch refuses, and the timers that publish were cancelled before the wipe — and one still out is cut; a fetch can still be made while logged out, so every login shuts the pool again before it provisions the next identity; the cost is one fresh connection for the next identity. Profile publishes build a manager of their own per call, and the live session's fanout drives use a pool of their own, closed with the session. Of what a relay can observe or the next identity's engine is started from, two things outlive the logout: the mounted shell's set of circles to re-subscribe, held until onboarding — the only place a login runs — replaces the shell; and a stop given up on, whose core's sockets and REQs last until its bounded stop closes them and whose open file handles last until its last task ends. Each Blossom request builds a client of its own and drops it, so neither a connection nor a TLS session ticket of one identity's request is presented by the next identity's; the relay sockets build a TLS config of their own per connection, so they resume nothing across identities either. A location the deleted identity's session was still handling is merged into no cache: the wipe closes the location service's in-memory cache, and the event router forgets the identity at the logout's end, so a handler of an event that arrived under it drops the location whole; no other stop drops one — after a pause, a detach or a foreground restart the location service's own state decides, and a paused one persists the fix where it still holds the store (not on Android with background sharing on, where the store is handed to the foreground service) and merges nothing into its closed cache. This becomes false if a SharedPreferences key is added without a decided fate, if the tile-cache wipe is dropped from the path, if the stop behind the latch is, if the detector's reset, the wedge clear, the router's identity fence or the pool's close is, if a login is reached from outside onboarding, or if a provider outside that set reads an identity-scoped value while it is built.

invariants.title: Leaf keys do not rotate on a timer (M5)
invariants.statement: No production file drives an MLS re-key on a schedule. The self-update provider that once did was a documented no-op and was DELETED with Unit E. So MLS epoch keys advance on a real membership change, one's own join or an explicit user repair - never periodically.

invariants.title: The profile pool overlaps no other relay plane, and the location pool none either
invariants.statement: profile_relay_pool_default() has exactly eight entries, PRODUCTION_DISCOVERY_RELAYS exactly six and PRODUCTION_LOCATION_RELAYS exactly eight. The profile and discovery sets are disjoint by construction; the profile pool is disjoint from the account seed defaults, which carry kind-1059 traffic and the kind-445 of circles whose relays came from them, and host-disjoint from the location pool, which carries the kind-445 of the circles Haven creates; and the location pool is host-disjoint from the seed and the discovery plane too, one registrable domain per entry. Since 2026-10-31 the profile pool also shares no operator with the account seed (wss://nostr.mom, nos.lol's operator, retired) and gives no operator two slots (wss://nostr.bitcoiner.social, offchain.pub's operator, retired) — recorded, not tested. invariants.title: No published event names the profile relays
invariants.statement: RelayType::Profile::to_kind() returns None, so no NIP-65 kind-10002 (or any other event) is ever built that serializes the profile relay list; this becomes false the moment Profile maps to a publishable kind or the list is written into an event's tags.

invariants.title: Profile lookups ask one relay about one person, bounded at two relays
invariants.statement: Every kind-0 filter carries exactly one author, no p tag and kind 0 only; each author resolves to its own assigned relay by salted rendezvous hash, and PROFILE_MAX_RELAY_RANK = 2 caps the retry ladder — so a lookup discloses an author to at most two of the eight. This becomes false if authors are batched into one filter, if the rank cap is raised, or if a fetch fans out beyond the assignment.

invariants.title: The assignment salt is zeroized, redacted and destroyed with the identity
invariants.statement: The per-install salt is ZeroizeOnDrop, renders redacted in Debug, never crosses the FFI, and is destroyed by BOTH the profile-delete path (wipe_all_profiles drops the row) and the logout wipe (the user_settings row is its only persistence, so deleting the circles.db file set takes it with it); this becomes false if a second identity on the same device can inherit the first's salt.

invariants.title: Two contacts can be assigned the same profile relay (P1)
invariants.statement: Assignment hashes the pubkey against a per-install salt with no knowledge of roster membership, so for a small circle several members genuinely can land on one pool relay; the spreading property is statistical, not an invariant.

invariants.title: Publishing your own profile reaches every usable pool relay (P2)
invariants.statement: publish_metadata targets the entire usable profile pool (it fails closed on an empty relay set rather than narrowing), so every pool relay learns (our pubkey, our IP) on every save; a subset publish would make the user invisible to peers assigned elsewhere.

event_kinds.note: Published to the whole usable pool via publish_metadata.

invariants.title: The eight profile relays are contacted unconditionally and see the device's IP (P3)
invariants.statement: usable_profile_relays() unions the eight defaults back in on every resolution, so the pool is contacted even when every user-chosen relay is private and a removal in Settings does not take effect; what the missing kind-10002 buys is only that relays OUTSIDE the pool get no public pointer to it. The relays Haven picks for a new circle from the location pool are recorded in the contamination ledger as CircleRouting, like any circle's relays, so none of them can enter the resolved profile pool; the curated eight are host-disjoint from the location pool, so that record never removes one of them.

invariants.title: The profile-relay pairing is durable by design (P5)
invariants.statement: The per-install salt is minted once and never rotated on a schedule, because each rotation would disclose every contact to an additional relay; the accepted cost is that the assigned relay accumulates a durable record that this IP keeps asking about this pubkey. The pairing still shifts for roughly 1/N of authors whenever the resolved pool changes.

invariants.title: Every host Haven contacts sees the real IP (P6)
invariants.statement: There is no Tor, proxy or onion transport: pool relays, circle relays, the tile provider and any host serving a co-member's profile picture observe the device's IP, and the co-member picture fetch happens automatically with no user action.

invariants.title: Relay exposure already incurred cannot be undone (P7)
invariants.statement: The contamination ledger is append-only, and Welcome-delivery relays from before the change were never persisted so refresh_contamination_ledger cannot fold them in; the UI can therefore only warn about an overlap it knows of, and excluding relays can shrink the profile pool below its usable floor. The relays Haven picks for a new circle from the location pool are recorded as CircleRouting at the create, before any Welcome is sent, as any circle's relays are; a pool entry never picked is never recorded. The pick's hard exclusion reads the ledger's non-CircleRouting rows, and the ledger keeps only the FIRST source a relay was recorded under, so a relay first recorded as a circle's that the user later put on — and then removed from — their inbox is excluded only while it stays on a list: best-effort.
