invariants.title: An edit to the user's own profile is not merged onto a relay copy older than the dated own-profile row this device holds.
invariants.statement: A kind-0 is replaced whole, so every own-profile publish is the freshest known object with the edit applied. A relay may answer the merge-base read with a superseded copy of the user's own profile: it is genuinely signed, so verification admits it. (1) merge_base takes the relays' copy as the base only when it is at least as new as the dated own-profile row this device holds; an older answer is not built on, so fields removed since — a payment address, a photo, a name — are not signed back under the identity key. Ties go to the relays' copy, and the lower event id decides a tie between relays, as NIP-01 keeps it. (2) That row is written when a profile fetch caches the copy, when the read a sync or a retraction makes for its base finds a newer one (before the publish, so a publish that then fails still leaves the row at the newest copy read), when a relay acknowledges a publish, and as the blank's record when the profile is deleted — dated as the blank is, written only after a relay acknowledged the blank and in one transaction with the record of its publication, so a relay that never took the blank can neither get the deleted profile cached again nor get the next edit built on it. Once written from an event the row records that event's whole metadata object, the fields Haven does not model included. (3) sync_own_profile and remove_my_profile_picture both resolve their base this way; when no relay serves the profile the base is the cached row, and a photo removal with neither a relay copy nor a dated row publishes nothing — never an empty or name-only profile over one this device cannot see. Outside this promise: a device holding no dated row (a fresh import of the key, or the first edit after the storage reset before a fetch has landed) builds on whatever the answering relays serve; and a process killed between a relay's acknowledgement and the local write has published a profile its row does not record, so until a fetch serves that profile back the row is older than what the device signed. Reverting merge_base to prefer any fetched copy, resolving the own read by arrival order, dropping the cache of the copy read before a publish, wiping the own row on deletion without recording the blank, or publishing a removal built on nothing, falsifies this.

invariants.title: A photo removal or profile deletion a profile relay did not acknowledge is left owed, and after such a removal the status line never reads up to date.
invariants.statement: Peers read a profile from the pool relays their own install is assigned, so a relay that did not take the kind-0 without the picture goes on serving the photo to them. (1) remove_my_profile_picture publishes to the whole usable pool and records the row, the publish and the coverage in one transaction (commit_profile_sync). Unless every relay it was sent to acknowledged it, the removal is not recorded as synced: with nothing else pending, the profile it published becomes a new pending version, partly published, with the retry ladder advanced; with an edit pending — queued before the removal or saved while it was being published — nothing is added, because that edit's own sync republishes the whole profile to the whole pool, and the edit is not reported as partly published when no relay was sent it. (2) The next due sync publishes the newest copy of the profile it reads — the profile without the picture, unless a strictly newer copy has appeared since — to every pool relay again, on the same persisted backoff as any partially acknowledged save and never at once: the backoff is dated when the removal is recorded, not when it began, and the status re-read that follows a removal neither starts nor queues a sync while one is in flight. Only a full acknowledgement clears it. (3) After such a removal the status line never reads up to date: it shows the partial state when the removal, or an edit it carried, is the version owed, and the pending edit's own state when an edit it did not carry is what will take it to the pool. (4) delete_my_public_profile leaves the blank it published owed in the same way, by the same statement (write_unqueued_publish_owed), in the transaction that wipes the cache (wipe_all_profiles); the retry publishes a blank again and no field of the deleted profile, even when the relay that refused the blank is the only one to answer the retry's read. Outside this promise: a relay that never acknowledges keeps the state at partial, and every retry pass signs a NEW kind 0 with a new public created_at for the whole pool — at most four passes in the first hour and then one per six hours, only while the app is opened, with no cap until every pool relay acknowledges or that relay leaves the pool (owner decision owed); a relay no longer in this install's usable pool is never sent the removal, and the outbox reads synced without it; a removal or deletion no relay acknowledged fails and records nothing; the kind-5 that accompanies a deletion is sent once; nothing in the app calls the deletion yet; and the hosted image file is not deleted (INV-P-PROFILE-REMOVAL-IS-NOT-DELETION). Recording a partially acknowledged removal or blank as synced, marking a pending edit published by it, dating the backoff from before the publish, republishing without the backoff, building the retry on an older copy a relay still serves, or dropping the status re-read after a removal, falsifies this.

invariants.title: MLS, circle and sync state are SQLCipher-encrypted on disk
invariants.statement: The sync-state and relay-state tables, and the `commit_notes` and `restage_waits` tables that hold what became of a circle's changes and how long a refused eviction waits, are unreadable in the raw database file without the keyring-held key, and an account wipe leaves nothing decryptable behind; this becomes false if a table is written outside the encrypted database or the wipe stops deleting the file set.

invariants.title: The map-tile cache is encrypted, capped at seven days, and wiped on identity deletion
invariants.statement: Tile blobs are stored only as SQLCipher-encrypted rows keyed by (style,z,x,y,retina) with the Stadia api_key stripped in Dart before the FFI, kTileMaxRetention is seven days and is the value the privacy copy quotes, and the wipe runs inside NostrIdentityService.deleteIdentity; this becomes false if a raw URL or api_key reaches the store, if the retention constant and the copy diverge, or if the wipe leaves the delete path.

invariants.title: The member directory records people, never which circle they came from
invariants.statement: member_directory carries exactly six columns — pubkey, is_current, last_shared_day, tier, rank_key, purge_after — and is WITHOUT ROWID, so it stores no implicit arrival-order counter either; no statement naming that table may also name a circle, group or MLS identifier; sync_co_members writes the UNION across all circles in one pass, so no row is attributable to a circle even by write timing. This becomes false if the table gains such a column by DDL or by a migration ALTER, if it regains a rowid (each pass inserts its NEW pubkeys in sorted order, so a descending pubkey step between consecutive rowids marks a batch boundary — a circle's roster), if a companion table re-creates the person-to-circle join beside it, or if a second writer outside the directory storage module inserts one.
invariants.residual: NO CIRCLE IDENTIFIER IS STORED; a limited circle inference is still available to an adversary holding the decrypted database. Everyone who leaves in the same day bucket freezes on the same last_shared_day, so a departure COHORT is visible, and for a user with few circles that cohort often IS one circle's roster. Day bucketing raises the cost of that re-partition and does not eliminate it (docs/MEMBER_PICKER_PLAN.md §6.1, which drops first_seen_day AND updated_day — the two columns that carried departure timing — along with second-granularity stamps and, since the WITHOUT ROWID conversion, the implicit rowid, precisely because each of them made it cheap). The bucket does not cross the FFI either: DirectoryEntryFfi carries pubkey_hex, npub and tier and nothing else, so the cohort stamp is legible only to someone reading the decrypted table directly, never to the UI layer. Scope: for CURRENT circles the same adversary can already read the full partition out of the engine's session.sqlite, so the directory only adds partition information for circles whose other rows delete_circle has already cascaded away.

invariants.title: A departed co-member is deleted from the directory three days later
invariants.statement: DIRECTORY_RETENTION_DAYS is 3 (259 200 s, owner decision D3, reduced from a drafted 7); a co-member absent from the union freezes at purge_after = (last_shared_day + 3) * 86400 and is removed by prune_expired_directory_members DELETING the row, never by a read hiding it, and a deliberate removal in either direction deletes the row immediately. The deadline binds the DISK, not only the display: the purge runs at every process start (CircleManager::new, a bare DELETE needing no MLS session and no roster read), inside the ranked read's own transaction before it selects, and in every reconcile — so the three days hold on an install that never opens the picker and never reconciles. Every one of those sweeps is the same comparison against the DEVICE WALL CLOCK — chrono::Utc::now() at process start, DateTime.now() marshalled as now_unix_secs for the ranked read and the reconcile — with no monotonic floor anywhere in the path, so the deadline binds only while that clock does. This becomes false if the constant changes, if an expired row is filtered out of a read instead of deleted, or if any of those three sweeps stops running.
invariants.residual: TWO RESIDUALS, BOTH IRREDUCIBLE AT THIS LAYER AND BOTH NOW OWNER-ACCEPTED RATHER THAN OPEN (decision D9, 2026-08-28, docs/MEMBER_PICKER_PLAN.md §10). (1) THE DEADLINE IS ENFORCED BY THREE ON-DEMAND SWEEPS, NOT BY A TIMER. An expired row is deleted at the next process start, at the next ranked read, or at the next reconcile — whichever comes first — and no read can return one, because the read sweeps inside its own transaction before it selects. What remains is the interval between the deadline and the next of those events on a device where the app never runs at all: the row is still on disk, unread by anything, until the process that would read it starts and erases it first. THAT ENFORCEMENT MODEL IS A DECISION, NOT AN INTERIM STATE: a timer and a background wake were both considered and declined under D9, because they buy the earlier deletion of a row nothing can read — the ranked read sweeps inside its own transaction before it selects — at the price of periodic wakeups. (2) THE CLOCK IS UNTRUSTED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, and there is no monotonic floor anywhere in the path. A forward jump purges EARLY, which costs recent contacts and is self-healing for current members. A BACKWARD jump is the mirror case and is worse for the promise: purge_expired is DELETE ... WHERE purge_after < ?1, so a rolled-back clock makes every one of the three sweeps a no-op — expiry is not delayed but suspended — and because the ranked read's in-transaction sweep is that same comparison, a row past its window stays both STORED and RETURNABLE for as long as the clock reads earlier than its deadline. Closing this needs a trusted clock: SQLCipher offers no monotonic counter and a boot-relative clock does not survive a reboot, so it is stated rather than fixed, and D9 accepts it in the same breath as the sweep model; the eventual copy may not resolve it by promising a fixed wall-clock window. It is stated because a disclosure claiming a fixed window depends on it — and that copy (owner decision D6) has had no surface since the Settings → Privacy page was removed on 2026-08-29, which is why this entry carries no disclosure key. There is no wording for a copy-tie test to pin to DIRECTORY_RETENTION_DAYS; the constant itself stays test-enforced (retention_is_the_owner_decided_three_days). The drafted paragraph and its clause-by-clause constraints are preserved in docs/MEMBER_PICKER_PLAN.md D6.

invariants.title: The member directory exists only inside the encrypted circles.db
invariants.statement: The directory is stored only as rows in the SQLCipher-encrypted circles.db whose key lives in the platform keyring, and in no SharedPreferences/NSUserDefaults entry, flutter_secure_storage item or sidecar file — so deleting the circles.db file set is the whole of the logout guarantee, and that deletion is DEVICE-LOCAL rather than absolute: on iOS the file set sits in the backed-up Documents directory and a same-device restore can reinstate a pre-logout snapshot (accepted deviation IOS-BACKUP, owner decision D8). This becomes false if any Rust, Dart or native path gives those rows a second home the logout deletion does not reach. The Dart half of the guard scans the directory surface discovered BOTH by filename convention and by import closure over the row/staged-pick/query-fold modules — a convention-only scan left member_avatar.dart, search_fold.dart, create_circle_page.dart and add_member_page.dart outside it, so a preferences write from any of them would have passed.
invariants.note: Status stays 'enforced' under owner decision D8 (2026-08-28), which accepts the iOS backup posture unchanged. What this invariant checks is that the rows have NO SECOND HOME — no preferences entry, no secure-storage item, no sidecar file, no second Connection — and an iOS backup is not a second home Haven writes: it is the OS copying the one home wholesale, still inside SQLCipher, still keyed by a ThisDeviceOnly Keychain item. The rows are never outside the encrypted container, which is the claim as titled, so a downgrade would report Haven's storage discipline as partly enforced when it is not partly anything, and would spend the ratchet's signal on the event this row exists to catch: the day a real second home appears. What the backup DOES falsify is the corollary — 'deleting the file set destroys it' read as absolute — and that corollary is now scoped in the statement and registered as deviation IOS-BACKUP, whose forbidden_claim binds the copy. Status 'accepted_deviation' was not available: rule 9 requires a disclosure, and the member-directory disclosure (decision D6) has had no surface since the Settings → Privacy page was removed on 2026-08-29; a zero-disclosure accepted deviation is permitted since that date, so filing one is a deliberate act, not done here.

invariants.title: FLAG_SECURE covers every Activity in the Android process
invariants.statement: HavenApplication.onCreate registers an activity-lifecycle callback that SETS FLAG_SECURE in onActivityCreated, no Activity sets it per-Activity, and the manifest still names HavenApplication — so the block covers the photo-crop Activity and any future plugin Activity, not just MainActivity. This becomes false if any one of those four links is removed.

invariants.title: On iOS only the app-switcher snapshot is blurred
invariants.statement: iOS offers no FLAG_SECURE equivalent, so nothing prevents an in-app screenshot or screen recording by a circle member; the only protection is the app-switcher blur, installed on applicationWillResignActive (not didEnterBackground), covering the window itself, removed and re-armed only on applicationDidBecomeActive, with no UIApplicationSceneManifest that would stop UIKit calling those callbacks. This becomes false if any one of those links is removed.

invariants.title: The camera is used only by the QR scanner

invariants.title: Location is encrypted on the device, readable only by the circle
invariants.statement: A location update is MLS-encrypted client-side before any network write and decrypts only under the originating circle's epoch keys; a member of another circle holding the same ciphertext cannot read it. This becomes false if any plaintext coordinate is written to a relay or if cross-group decryption starts succeeding.

invariants.title: Haven runs no server of its own for circle traffic
invariants.statement: Identity-plane publishes (the kind-10050 and kind-10002 lists, KeyPackages) target exactly the user's own stored relay lists; a circle's kind-445 goes to that circle's relays, which for a circle Haven creates without named relays are three third-party relays drawn from the curated location pool (PRODUCTION_LOCATION_RELAYS, INV-R-CIRCLE-RELAYS-FROM-LOCATION-POOL) and for any other circle the relays its creator chose; and the live-sync engine connects only to configured relays — each circle's relays and the inbox list — never a gossip-discovered one. There is no Haven-operated endpoint in the location path. This becomes false if any publisher, engine client or curated relay list acquires a first-party destination.
invariants.residual: Nothing proves that no curated list holds a Haven-operated relay: the location and profile pools' operators are recorded when the pools are vetted, not tested. And the user chooses none of: the eight profile relays and six discovery relays (contacted unconditionally, not removable, INV-P-P3), the three location-pool relays Haven picks for each circle it creates (no setting edits them), the Blossom host (hardcoded to blossom.primal.net) and the tile provider (hardcoded to Stadia). The copy claims no such choice: onboardingValueProp2Summary was reworded on 2026-10-31 from 'It runs on a relay network you choose.' — false once Haven picks a circle's relays — to 'No central server. It runs on independent relays.' (extended on 2026-11-04 with 'Many people run them, so no single company can switch it off.', which names no choice either), and relaySettingsBackendCaption names no choice either. Nothing fails if a curated list grows.

invariants.title: A relay can only be added over wss://
invariants.statement: The Rust storage boundary rejects a relay URL whose PARSED scheme is plaintext ws, however its text spells it (ws://, WS://, ws:host, ws:/host), regardless of what the Dart validator did, so no plaintext WebSocket relay can be persisted. The same single predicate on the parsed URL (relay::url_norm::may_dial) decides every other place a relay string is acted on: the publish and fetch validator, the live-sync engine's gate (a relay that fails it in a list the engine is handed fails that whole session start, or that circle's subscribe, with the engine's relay error — which names no relay — and is never handed to the engine client, so no standing subscription naming a circle is opened in the clear), the derivation of a circle's own relay list from its routing component (an entry another client's admin wrote that fails the predicate is dropped — the entry, never the list and never the component — at the join and at every later re-derivation, so it costs the circle that one relay and stops neither the circle's publishes, nor the relay update that repairs it, nor the engine for the device's other circles; a circle none of whose entries pass has no relay, and a publish for it ends in the typed all-relays-failed outcome with nothing dialled), the relay-list builders (a kind-10002 or kind-10050 list naming a plaintext relay is not built, so one is never advertised) and the validation of a circle's routing component before Haven writes one. A debug build's loopback opt-in, which a release cannot arm, is the one exception. This becomes false if the storage-side scheme check is relaxed to trust the UI, or if any of these decisions goes back to testing how the string begins.

tests.name: maps the insecure-scheme error to its localized message

invariants.title: A circle's relays are never on a loopback, private or link-local host
invariants.statement: Every path that takes a circle's relays from its routing component keeps only an entry another account's relay list may name (relay::manager::foreign_relay_dialable: wss to a host MDK's is_loopback_host and is_public_ip admit, a domain accepted unresolved apart from the loopback names; a debug build's ws loopback opt-in is the one exception): the join and every later re-derivation of the circle's own relay list (circle::manager::usable_relays) and the relays a commit or a location is frozen for (fanout_targets). A failing entry is dropped — the entry, never the list and never the component — and a circle none of whose entries pass has no relay. Haven never writes such an entry: a relay update naming one is refused (circle_relays) and so is a create whose caller named one (routing_of), in fixed text naming no relay and no host, before anything is recorded or staged; a create whose caller named no relays draws from the location pool (or its debug override) and leaves out every entry that fails the rule, and is refused (NoLocationRelay) only when no entry is left once that rule and the creator's own identity relays are applied; no log line names the host. This becomes false if any of these paths goes back to judging the scheme alone.
invariants.residual: A domain is accepted unresolved, so a name that resolves to a private address is still dialled, as it is for MDK's own reject_unsafe_relay_host (tracker T-GROUP-RELAY-HOSTS).

invariants.title: Roster and circle name rest on one confidentiality layer, not two
invariants.statement: Group-control kind-445s (commits and proposals) are MLS PublicMessage under the engine's PURE_PLAINTEXT_WIRE_FORMAT_POLICY — signed and integrity-protected but NOT MLS-encrypted — so the roster, member credentials (each member's Nostr identity pubkey), their 0xF2F1 identity proofs and the circle name carried inside them are protected by the outer exporter-keyed ChaCha20-Poly1305 wrap ALONE. Application messages are double-sealed: OpenMLS encrypts them unconditionally regardless of the wire-format policy, so a location sits inside an MLS PrivateMessage inside that same outer wrap.
invariants.residual: Nothing in this tree fails if an MDK bump changes the wire-format policy or the exporter derivation; the only levers are pinned_dependencies.mdk_rev and the grep-based check_no_exporter_label_override.sh. Upstream itself marks the policy WIRE_FORMAT_POLICY_REVIEW_REQUIRED ('Revisit Before External Rollout'). So the confidentiality of the circle's NAME and MEMBER LIST is single-layered while the location half is not — a future change could silently downgrade one and not the other.

event_kinds.note: Commits/proposals ride the same kind as application messages but a different MLS wire format.

invariants.title: Until the storage-reset notice is answered and the answer saved, Haven publishes no relay list and no KeyPackage
invariants.statement: The one-time storage reset (the MDK v0.10.4 migration) returns the relay-list publishing choices to their defaults. Until the user has answered the reset notice AND that answer was saved, Haven publishes neither of its relay lists (kind 10050 inbox, kind 10002 NIP-65) and no KeyPackage (kind 30443): every path that could publish one — the relay-list maintenance tick, the KeyPackage maintenance tick, and the user-edit publish — reads storage_reset_acknowledged and returns AwaitingResetAcknowledgement while it is false. A save that fails leaves the marker in place, so the hold stays and the notice is shown again; the snackbar that says so (storageResetAcknowledgeFailed) is therefore a promise the code keeps. It is NOT a promise that nothing is published: the public profile, invitations the user sends and location still go out, and the deletion of a KeyPackage's key at its not_after never waits for the notice. Publishing either list or a KeyPackage on any path while the marker exists, or clearing the hold without a saved answer, falsifies this.

invariants.title: A receive plane hands the engine kind-445 group messages and nothing else, so a circle is joined only when the user accepts its invitation
invariants.statement: Every event a receive plane delivers (the catch-up poll and live sync) passes the pre-auth screen in SessionManager::process_event, which refuses anything whose kind is not 445 before the engine sees it. The engine joins any Welcome it is handed, and a kind-1059 gift wrap is a Welcome envelope, so without the screen a relay could make this device join a circle its user never accepted simply by answering a group subscription with a gift wrap. A Welcome reaches the engine only through accept_welcome, after the user accepted the invitation Haven was holding. Removing the kind comparison, or adding a receive path that reaches the engine's ingest without it, falsifies this.

event_kinds.note: A COMPARISON, not a construction: the pre-auth kind screen at nostr/mls/manager.rs::screen_before_auth, which lets a kind-445 through and refuses every other kind as PreAuthRejection::Malformed. The constant is KIND_GROUP_MESSAGE (haven-core/src/nostr/event.rs). Kind 445 itself is built out of tree by the rev-pinned peeler.

invariants.title: A circle's mesh keys exist, in memory and at rest, only until the mesh deadline, and for the engine's own window of epochs
invariants.statement: A Bluetooth mesh packet is sealed under a key derived from a circle's group-event exporter secret at one epoch. Haven keeps that secret per circle for the epoch the engine stands stable on and the five before it (DEFAULT_MAX_PAST_EPOCHS) — in the session's key ring and in the mesh_keys table of the SQLCipher circles-v2.db — and ONLY until the deadline user_settings.mesh_on_until, which is never more than twelve hours ahead of the session's clock (MESH_ON_MAX_MS) and which a clock set back does not move further away while the process lives. Every key and the deadline are deleted, in one transaction, when mesh is turned off; when the deadline has passed, at the open of the store, at the next engine batch, at the KeyPackage maintenance tick, before mesh is turned on again and, only while a mesh engine runs in the process, at a mesh drive and at the first bridge entry after it; a circle's keys go with the circle; a staged epoch's secret is never read; and the store overwrites what it deletes (secure_delete). With mesh never turned on, nothing is derived and nothing is stored. Keeping a key past the deadline, storing one with mesh off, or widening the window beyond the engine's falsifies this.
invariants.residual: It is a second at-rest copy of a secret MDK's own store already holds for the same epochs, under the same keyring service. The rollback journal of the deleting transaction is unlinked, not wiped, and flash storage keeps no promise about overwritten pages; both hold ciphertext under the database key. Across a process restart the time left is the wall clock's word alone: a wall clock set back while Haven is not running lengthens it, never past twelve hours from the open. A process that owns the session and never runs the mesh engine keeps the keys current until the deadline. Tracker row T-MESH-EXPORTER carries the upstream ask that would let the ring store nothing.

invariants.title: A location reaches the Bluetooth mesh at one place, after the checks a relay send passes, and the relay send waits for nothing of the mesh's
invariants.statement: The mesh has no sealing code of its own. A sealed location is handed to it by one call, SessionManager::mesh_offer, made once in the location's own send after its send-time checks and before its relay send: an event the relay path would not send never reaches the mesh. The hand-off waits for nothing — a lock is only tried, the store is not written, and a packet that cannot be left is dropped — so a location's relay send answers the same, and a relay is sent the same frames, with mesh on and off. Whatever silences a circle on the relay path (an epoch change, a commit or proposal of this device's recorded, fetched input held unread, a leave asked, sharing stopped, the circle's end, mesh off) empties that circle's outbox slot before the engine can emit from it, and a session that opens while the engine runs is handed to it with the last session's outbox purged. A second call site, a hand-off before the send-time checks, or a relay send that waits on the mesh falsifies this.

invariants.title: The mesh hands the engine only verified application messages of the epoch whose key opened them, calls no relay and changes nothing a relay is asked
invariants.statement: A packet the mesh received reaches the MLS engine only if it opens under a key of one of this device's circles, the event rebuilt from it passes Event::verify() (id and signature, Security Rule 16), and — checked before the engine sees anything — it is an application message whose inner epoch is the epoch of the key that opened the packet. A commit, a proposal, and an application message of any other epoch are read and dropped, so no group state changes by radio. The drive calls no relay whatever the engine hands back, so when a relay hears from this device never follows from a packet anyone in radio range can replay; and it changes nothing a relay is asked: the mesh owns no cursor and no floor, an update it brings is recorded nowhere the relay path reads what it has seen, it arms no history walk and stamps no inbound arrival. A circle with a commit of this device's pending, or holding fetched input unread, takes nothing in, and what waits for it is bounded per circle. Skipping verify(), admitting a commit or proposal, or sending to a relay from the drive falsifies this.

invariants.title: A location sealed for the Bluetooth mesh alone is sent to no relay by any call, and nothing is sealed for a mesh that is off
invariants.statement: A fix sealed for the mesh alone (Publishing::seal_for_mesh, the bridge's seal_location_for_mesh_driven) is recorded as mesh-only in the session, in the hold that seals it: the send that follows hands it to the mesh as the packet format no member passes on to a relay, sends it to no relay and answers MeshOnly, whatever its caller does with the event, and a process that did not seal it sends it nowhere. The seal itself calls no relay, makes no commit and drives nothing; every hold that holds a relay seal holds it. With mesh off — and, at the bridge, with no engine running to carry it — nothing is sealed and the engine is not asked. A mesh-only seal that reaches a relay, or a seal made with mesh off, falsifies this.
invariants.residual: One caller exists, and only in a build with the HAVEN_MESH define, which no shipped build passes: an iOS background burst whose relay receive failed, with mesh on and the burst still owning the wake (BackgroundBurstCoordinator, docs/BLUETOOTH_MESH_PLAN.md §7.7 R1). A burst the foreground took back or whose consent was withdrawn, any such burst with mesh off, and every burst of a build without the define seal nothing: 'a burst that cannot receive publishes nothing' still describes those. A fix so sealed is sealed at the last epoch the phone knows: a member removed by a commit the phone could not fetch, holding the old keys and within radio range, can read it until the phone next completes a receive; and each such seal spends one MLS message generation.

invariants.title: A passed-on mesh update tells the circle's relays that a member is offline and near the device that passed it on
invariants.statement: With the Bluetooth mesh on, a fellow member's location this device took in by mesh is passed on to the circle's relays: that member's own sealed event, byte for byte, once; only behind this device's own location send of the same circle, to the relays that took it; only in a drive whose relay receive completed before the send, which is the caller's word (in Dart, 'received' only from an iOS background burst whose own relay receive was answered to the end — a backlog wait that settled behind an open or a start that succeeded, or, where no live plane exists, a catch-up that completed; 'not received' from every foreground tick and one-shot publish, which receive nothing first, from a seal for the mesh alone, and from the Android service, whose cycle publishes before it fetches — so nothing is passed on from Android or from the foreground; and no build without the HAVEN_MESH define, which no shipped build passes, has a mesh to bring anything); only an update the engine read for the first time from packets that all mark it as one a member may pass on; only while a location this device sealed at the same epoch could itself be sent; one attempt a relay, never retried, its answer read by nothing; at most one a member each 72 seconds, four a send, none begun once passing on has run for one send's time, and none later than 218 seconds after it was sealed. Those bounds are tested. What they do not hide is the accepted cost: the event arrives tens of seconds after its created_at and off this device's own rhythm, so a relay of the circle — and any subscriber of its routing id — can infer that some member of that circle is offline and within radio reach of this device's network address, and when the sender reaches the relay too, one event from two connections links their addresses.

invariants.title: The mesh engine and every packet it carries live in memory only, and the first entry after the twelve-hour deadline drops them
invariants.statement: The mesh engine's store, its per-packet records, its outbox and its queue of unread packets are never written to disk. One engine a process, reached only through mesh_run — by every entry under with_mesh, by every start under mesh_take — which before every engine call checks the deadline and applies what the session left for the engine — an offer for as long as its event still has by the wall clock and never longer than a location lives, a purge at once. Applying it runs none of the engine's timers, and neither does anything else an entry that holds a session calls: such an entry is made right after a relay send, so the engine emits, renews its greeting and decides about links only at the radio's entries, and an emission slot that fell due is served by the radio's next entry with what waits then — never with what was withdrawn meanwhile. The engine's clock is read in Rust for every entry and never handed in by a caller: monotonic and counting the time the device sleeps (CLOCK_BOOTTIME on Android and Linux, CLOCK_MONOTONIC on Apple targets), so no change of the wall clock moves a packet's lifetime or the deadline. Nobody turns mesh off at its deadline; the first entry after it does, before it runs anything: the engine is dropped with every packet it held, and an entry that holds the session deletes every key. That holds for the entries a radio drives the engine through, which hold no session and can reach none: each checks the deadline first, and one that finds it passed drops the engine and leaves the keys to the next entry that holds a session. The radio's service may start an engine with no session on its own word, once a process and only while no session has spoken in that process: not after a session opened or made an entry, mesh on or off; not after mesh was turned off, from the moment the engine is dropped; not after an engine ended at its deadline; not after the identity was deleted or an engine call panicked. That engine is keyless, runs for at most twelve hours, and is overruled by the first session that opens: its deadline is brought no later than that session's, which is at once when that session's mesh is off, and from then the service's word starts nothing. Turning mesh off, and deleting the identity, drop the engine first. The engine's lock is never held across an await. Persisting a packet, taking the engine's clock from a caller, running the engine after its deadline, running an engine timer from an entry that holds a session, or an engine started on the service's word after a session has spoken or a second time in one process falsifies this.
invariants.residual: With no entry at all the engine sits in memory past its deadline — it can do nothing, since only an entry runs it — and is freed at the next entry or when the process ends; the keys then end by the session's own wall-clock paths. No test can show that the clock runs while a device sleeps: that rests on the platform's documented behaviour (clock_gettime(3) on Apple, clock_gettime(2) on Linux), and on any other target the clock may stop with the machine. No radio is built: the entries a radio drives the engine through exist, an Android build exports them as JNI symbols (mesh_jni.rs), and no Kotlin declares or calls one, so nothing links the engine to another phone in any build, and nothing starts an engine with no session. Until the first session opens, an engine so started would run on the service's word alone, with the store's own deadline unread: for twelve hours at most with no session at all, once a process. Nothing in Rust bounds that across process restarts — each new process takes the service's word once more — so the bound there is the service's own stored deadline, which is not built. Open and not closed: where a power manager suspends the processor between the location service's wakes (unverified), the radio's own entries fall inside those wakes, so emission instants can still follow relay sends there; and an engine's first slot is drawn from the instant it starts, which follows a relay send when a session's resume starts it. Dart starts and resumes the engine only in a build with the HAVEN_MESH define, which no shipped build passes, and there a turn-on asks a radio that has no native end, fails and stores nothing.

invariants.title: The mesh keeps four counts and nothing else about its use, shows them, and logs none; no identifier crosses the bridge
invariants.statement: What the device records of its mesh use is four integers in user_settings of the SQLCipher circles-v2.db: two lifetime totals — updates from this device's circles the engine read for the first time out of a mesh packet, and packets this device carried, could not open and sent on — and what each read when mesh was last turned on. No timestamp, and no breakdown by circle, peer or packet. Each update and each passed-on packet is counted once, whatever is replayed; a total never decreases; turning mesh on starts the since-on pair and nothing else does; a reset forgets all four; deleting the identity deletes them with the store. The exact counts are shown to the user and never logged: the types that carry them have no Debug, the mesh's part of the bridge writes no log line, and what crosses the bridge is a fieldless state, bools, those counts, the time left until the deadline and the locations every receive path already hands over — never a packet, packet id, key, epoch, group id, slot or relay, and never how many phones are linked, only whether one is.

invariants.title: No Dart code calls a Bluetooth mesh entry unless the build has the HAVEN_MESH define, and what it calls there changes no relay send
invariants.statement: The Dart side of the Bluetooth mesh is compiled behind const meshEnabled = bool.fromEnvironment('HAVEN_MESH'), off unless a build passes the define; no build script or workflow passes it. With it off no Dart code calls a mesh entry whatever is asked of the mesh — the service provider answers null and the Android service's isolate builds no mesh service — so mesh cannot be turned on, no mesh key is stored and nothing is passed on to a relay; and with it off, as on every platform but Android with it on, there is no radio, no radio channel is touched, and nothing of the mesh is on screen: the map shell's layers, the own-location layer and the Settings page are what they are without it. With it on: the engine of a mesh an earlier process left on is resumed once a session, before any other entry made with that session; a mesh drive rides a foreground publish tick behind its relay publishes, an iOS background burst behind its relay receive and the Android service's cycle behind its relay fetch, and adds no wake of its own; what a drive read goes where a relay drive's replay goes, and where the map polls the relays the drive does not make it fetch; no relay send waits for a drive, and a drive that failed changes no relay link, its order or what it answers, nor does a relay publish wait for the word a publish pass gives the map's ripple or change with what becomes of it; turning background sharing off withdraws what waits to go out by mesh; where there is a radio, mesh is turned on only with both its engine and its radio — nothing is stored before the radio's permission, the caller's confirmation and Bluetooth have been asked, and a radio that does not start is stopped and takes the engine, its keys and its deadline with it — turning off stops the radio first and the engine whatever the radio did, a report of the radio in the middle of the user's own change starts and stops nothing and is acted on behind it, a radio that will not come back is asked once before mesh goes off, no entry of the radio is waited for past its bound, and a logout and the retry of its wipe stop the radio before the wipe; on screen the first turn-on shows the disclosure, and then the phone's Bluetooth name once it can be read, before anything is stored, and the four counts are shown and never logged; and the mesh's Dart code writes no log line. A mesh entry called or a radio channel touched with the flag off, a key left stored behind a radio that did not start, a relay publish that waits for or fails with a mesh drive, or a drive that makes the device ask a relay falsifies this.
invariants.residual: In a build with the define the mesh button is on the map on Android alone, and the radio's channels have no native end: no radio starts in any build, and a turn-on there asks the channel, fails with fixed words and stores nothing. The ripple on the user's own dot follows the hand-off of a location to the mesh and not the radio's emission, so someone watching the unlocked screen learns when a location was handed over. The phone's Bluetooth name is held by the widget that shows it, for as long as it is on screen. The disclosure's assurances — that a phone carrying a packet cannot read it, and that a phone in range or connected cannot tell what packets say or whose they are — rest on the core's packet envelope and link encryption (haven-core/src/mesh), which have no row of their own here yet: that row, and the rows for what the radio itself gives away, are owed with the radio. An engine that would not stop keeps its keys until a later reconcile, or the deadline. A burst does not wait for its mesh drive, so an update the drive takes in after that circle's own send is not passed on by that burst. A drive and a seal both take the one engine lock in Rust, and a teardown waits for a drive in flight as for every driven entry, so the session is never released under an engine call. A device with no circle eligible to publish arms no tick and drives the mesh at none. MapShell's handlers are not mounted host-side: that a burst is handed the mesh, that the start-up reads the mesh state, and that the start-up and every resume reconcile the engine with the radio, are pinned from the source.
